THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History
Interview with
Lee Young by Patricia Willard
Reel 1
November 8, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
MS .WILLARD: November 8, 1977. The Oral History, with Lee Young.
Lee, I see in two biographies on you, in the Chilton and Feather books, that your full name is -- well, you pronounce it.
Leonidas Leonidis.
Leonidas. Leonidis. It's a Greek pronunciation, isn't it?
Yes, it is. Leonidas Leonidis Raymond Young, Senior. I also gave that name to someone else.
Yes, I've heard about ...
To get even!
You mean you haven't enjoyed that name?

Well, I haven't used that name. The only time that name was ever really used was when I was in Junior High School. All the teachers called me Leonidas Leonidis. But when I got to high school, it was Lee, because, you know, it'd kind of a difficult name, and they pronounced it Leonetis, Leonatis, anything but Leonidis Leonidas ... so ...
Well, how did your parents happen to name you Leonidas Leonidas?
Well, my father was a schoolteacher --

he was a professor of music, and he also taught history at the University of New Orleans, and he was in to Greek, I guess, and you know, I read about Leonidas incidentally. You know, Leonidas was a great warrior or something; he held the bridge with a thousand men, he held 10,000 soldiers -- and when you, you know, when you're very young, that's kind of interesting, because you can just imagine the warriors fighting and this guy holding all these people at bay, for three days, I think it was!
So at that time, I guess I was kind of proud of Leonidas. Probably got beat up an awful lot, because of that.
You identified with it?
Yeah, I guess you could say that.
You were born March 7, 1917?
Yeah, in New Orleans.
New Orleans.
New Orleans, right.
And your father's name was William ...
William Handy Young.
-- Handy, H-a-n-d-y?
Uh huh.
And he was a band leader?
Yes, he was.
And he also was a school teacher?

He was a school teacher. Yeah. My father played -- I think he was a very interesting man. You don't, I guess you don't really know too much about it when you're growing up -- I guess you just don't realize what your parents really are a lot of times. Especially if they are talented.

But as I grew up and started playing music, I think it'd be interesting for me to note and to tell you the type of instruments that my father played. He played the instruments that was needed in the band; in the orchestra at that time. I heard, and had seen him play the piano, he played piano, he played trumpet, he played trombone, he played violin, he played Sousaphone, he played Mellophone, he played bass, string bass, and all of these instruments -- to say nothing about saxophone. Saxophone, I think, was his instrument.
He played all of the saxaphones?

Yes. You know, if you can play one saxaphone, generally you can play the other, you know -- it's just a matter of -- he was playing C Melody, I think, at the time, which I think is extinct now. They don't have C Melody instruments any more, but he was really a great musician.
And he taught, other than Lester, the ones that you would know. I think if you're talking about history, he

used to talk about -- what was that man's name? Clarence Williams. My father taught Clarence Williams, and I think you'd have to go back a ways to see who this was, but he was a pianist, and I've since -- I read of him, you know, but he was -- I don't know when, it must've been in the 20's or in the 18's or something. A little research on it would probably get him ... but he -- my dad taught him.

He also taught Cootie Williams. Cootie Williams traveled with us when I was a little kid on the carnival -- we used to go on carnivals, and Cootie, it seems to me that my dad got him in Birmingham or Mobile, Alabama. We were with a carnival called "Lackman and Carson Show". That's when the carnivals used to have a railroad car; they would have the Pullman cars and they would have dining cars, and you used to travel just as the circuses did.
And we had one of the shows on the carnival. And Lester and my sister and my mother and my dad - Lester and my sister played in the band; my sister also played saxaphone, Irma.
Your sister -- Lester was 8 years older than you, is that right?
Yeah, uh huh.
And Irma, what was she?
She's 4 or 5 -- you know, but it's like 8 years and 4 years; that type of thing. But speaking of

the carnivals, before I get off that -- as I said before, I think my dad, I think he got Cootie in Mobile, Alabama or Birmingham, Alabama, and then in later years when we were on the way from Minnesota -- and I'm skipping some of that -- to come west, we were in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and that's the first time we met Ben Webster.

Well, Ben Webster came to my dad as a piano player, and at the time my dad needed a saxophone, and Ben couldn't play but two keys -- he could play in B flat and C on the piano, and so my dad told him he was not a piano -- he was not a pianist. Ben and some fellow from Chicago -- his name was -- he was a violin player, and they came and so my dad got him with Lester and taught Ben to play saxophone, because he needed a saxophone player.
You say he got him in with Lester, so he learned by playing along with Lester?

Yeah. Oh yes, uh huh. They used to practice together. But you see, at the time, Lester played alto and Ben was playing tenor, because, see, my sister was not going to play any more, and so she was playing -- and so she was gonna sing with the band.
But now getting back to the carnival, if you want to know what I was doing with the carnivals then, which you may want to know, I was a blackface comedian.
At what age?
About ... well I was. Let's go back to the beginning. The first thing I can remember, almost from all of my life I can remember that I was in show business. Okay?

I remember very little about New Orleans; very, very little -- nothing. All I remember is playing under the house and that type of thing, but I was like 5 years old when I left New Orleans, so my dad took the three of us -- it was a separation -- and he took the 3 of us and we went on the road.

Now there is a gap in between that I have no recollection of, never have because I'm not sure if there is a gap. Because all I can ever remember is the next thing I knew, I was traveling and I was singing and dancing. I couldn't give you a clue how I learned to dance, other than looking at people dancing, you know? That's how I think I learned.

But years later when we were traveling on the carnivals, they had some great, great dancers -- and I remember, I saw Bill Bojangles Robinson with a Medicine Show. I don't know if you're familiar with what Medicine Shows were. Medicine Shows were things that just went around from town to town with a wagon, and they would open up there and they'd have some kind of little stage built there. Well, Bojangles used to dance in wooden shoes, you know? He would dance in
wooden shoes.
What kind of wooden shoes?
Well, they had -- dancers used to dance in wooden shoes at the time, that I'm speaking of. You know, this was ... I must have been 6 or 7 years old.
Were they a special dancing shoe? Not like a Dutch wooden shoe?
No. No. They were really dancing shoes, and instead of having taps on the heels and the toes, well, the shoe in its entirety was a wooden shoe.
The top was wood, too?

No. No. It would be leather, and just the soul would be wood. And they used to -- I don't really know, but I would imagine that's what they were talking about with some dance they called the 'Clog'? I don't know whether you ever heard of that, you know, but they did that with wooden shoes.
Let's see if I can get it chronologically for you. Let's see, after we left the carnivals, this is just what I can remember, you know? That we were on the TOBA circuit, which is ...
TOBA stood for what?
TOBA stood for 'Tough On Black Actors'. That's what it stood for. And you know, on that circuit, I think it was a Godsend, really, for a professional black

performers at the time, because that was probably the only chance they had to work, other than working on carnivals and circuses, because they had the Keith Orpheum circuit then, and they had the Pantages circuit, which I think that was out west, but in the south and the midwest, for a black performer -- Ethel Waters came off of it, I don't know if you've heard of the Whitman Sisters and those type of people. Butter Beans and Suzie ... they had a circuit that, I know we played Georgia, Florida, Texas, Louisiana, and you would work split week sometimes.

For instance, in Florida, I know we would play Tampa for three days and Pensacola for three days and that type of thing, but it would be in theatres -- and the theatres would always be packed. We'd play Oklahoma City, Tulsa, Oklahoma, and many of the really, the -- as I say, Bessie Smith was on TOBA, Mamie Smith was on TOBA -- and that was when I really learned to dance.

Because they used to have really great dances, and I remember -- I don't know whether it was Tulsa, Oklahoma City where they had a dance contest, where I can't remember how he spelled his name, but it was one that stuck out in my mind; his name was Jack Wiggins. Jack Wiggins was really a great dancer, and they had others that thought that they were great -- all of them thought that they were the greatest!
And so they would meet once in awhile and they

would have a dance contest, and the way the judges would judge them, they would go downstairs under the stage and they only had numbers; they would say, "This is number one dancing, this is number 4 or 5 dancing" -- and I'm sure they were doing that for clarity, you know, and the judges would stay downstairs and they would never see the dancers and they would make their decision when they came up and they would say who was the better dancer.
They judged on the basis of the sound?
Yes, that's right.
Just the sound.

Just the sound. And it's interesting, if you, you know -- if you danced and if you were a dancer, you really understand why, because you're not -- I think that they did that; it's very similar to what they do now in the record business, I think, you know, because if you go in to hear an artist -- or see an artist -- you would rather hear the artist, on tape than to go see the artist visually, because if she or he -- if they are showmen, they can sell you, you know?

But I think that was the same premise that the judges were using way back then, going under the stage, because maybe some guy had more facial expressions or something, and the guy who may have been the better dancer had no personality

at all -- but he wouldn't be judged on his personality; he would be judged on what he was doing with his feet, so, you know, I think that phase of it was very, very interesting -- but I used to dance and sing all the time, you know, on the TOBA circuit, and after we left the TOBA circuit, we moved to Minnesota -- to Minneapolis, and I was going to grammar school. But that's when my dad formed a band in Minneapolis. And, as a matter of fact, the Pettifords were also from Minneapolis because Lester used to hang out with them, you know, and I think we had like a 13-piece band, and many good musicians, but I quit traveling with them during school. I used to sing; I used to be the vocalist in the band, so during school, I would remain in Minneapolis, and then my dad and Lester and them would go out on the road.

But I don't think you ever heard a musician practice more or diligently than Lester did. At that time when we were in Minneapolis, you know, he was a young guy, because I was in grammar school, and his idol at the time was Frankie Trumbauer. A lot of people may not realize it, but he was around when Lester played alto.

And he used to play all of these Frankie Trumbauer records in his room, and I used to hear -- Frankie Trumbauer used to make a lot of records that was -- well, he was running over the horn, and all along, you know? It was like The Bouncing Ball that had funny titles like that. It just showed the dexterity and

his execution, more or less. But the guy used to practice all the time. Now ... from Minneapolis, like, on the way out here, when we stopped in Albuquerque, why, that's when I decided I wanted to play trombone.

Well, I think I bypassed something; I didn't tell you about -- we had a family band at one time, okay? We had cousins; let me see, my dad, my mother, my sister, my brother and myself -- and 2 cousins, and all of us played saxophone. It was a saxophone band. So some of that that you might see in some of the jazz books, where it says it was a saxophone trio; no, it wasn't a saxophone trio with Lester, my sister and I. It was my mother, my father and 2 cousins. One of them was called Cousin Sport and Cousin something, I don't know.
Boots?
Cousin Boots, that's right.
Jimmy Talbot told me that!

Jimmy Talbot tell you that? Well, Boots was his name. Well, it's a funny thing -- there's a funny story about it. Boots was the one that -- he played good saxophone, you know, and Lester, even as a kid, he loved the competition of playing his horn, and you know, during this time, they were wearing short pants.
And Cousin Boots was playing this dance, and Lester couldn't get in because he wanted to play -- he wanted to play against him. So he couldn't get in because Cousin Boots
had all the glory -- everybody thought that he was really great.

And Lester got to the dance somehow. I don't know how he got in to the dance, but he got in to the dance and he went up on the stand and he took his horn out then, and he just absolutely killed him, you know. He just absolutely killed him, and I'll never forget how Cousin Boots was gonna whip him, you know, was gonna take his belt off and whip him. That was the time when my mother interceded and, you know, told him it wasn't gonna happen because he said the kid embarrassed him, he came up there, you know, and was blowing in on his gig, you know -- I don't think they were using the term 'gig' then, but that's, you know, whatever he said -- that's what happened.

And then a peculiar thing about -- you know, when you're young, you're so foolish sometimes about you know, what a child thinks, and I think the reason I ended up playing the different instruments was because I really didn't want to play, you know? No. I wasn't like Lester. I really didn't want to play the instrument. I wanted to be out playing baseball and basketball, you know.

Well, in our house, you had to play an instrument or you know, that was it. You had to do that it. So I would say, "I want to play the trumpet" -- you know, ever since I was a baby, "Do you want to play a trumpet?" You know, and

the next day, he would come up with a trumpet. And I was thinking he couldn't get these instruments because I thought he was buying them, you know, not thinking that he was a music teacher and he could go downstairs -- go downtown, rather, to the music store and get an instrument. It would be trombone and And so he'd say, "You want a trombone? Okay, but you're gonna go to your room and you're gonna practice the trombone."
So, I think that accidentally, really, I got my musical knowledge from thinking that I wasn't gonna learn, you know? But there was no way not to learn with my dad.

I'll tell you a little funny story about rehearsing with my dad. He used to write things up on the blackboard for you. And he had this yardstick, but Lester had just marvelous ears, you know, and it really did run in the family, you know, because I have relative pitch -- you know, someone can play something and I can whistle it back to them, or whatever, you know -- I can do that now. But he was just uncanny, and he didn't like to read music. Well, Irma and I could read -- and Lester couldn't read very well because he didn't like to read. He liked to get with the records and he wanted to play with the records, but I'll never forget, my dad told him, "You got to learn to read or you won't get no thing. job playing big." You got to read this. But my dad could play.
So Lester was, he was too quick for him, and so I

think somewhere along the line my dad set a trap for him, because he didn't believe that Lester was really reading as fast as he was. So he used to write things up on the board for us to play, you know?

And we would ... I would play it, Irma, and I would read and play. And Lester would play it wrong, you know. And so my dad would pick up the horn and say, 'How can you play it like that? This is the way it goes.' Whatever, you know. And so he would give Lester the horn back and Lester would play ba ba dee doo dee, right?

But he was putting his ear on him, see? And so then my dad wrote somethig else up on the board and he -- and then he played it for Lester. No, Lester played it wrong; Lester played it wrong. Then my dad took the horn and he played it and he said, 'This is how it goes.' Ba Ba Doo Dee Doo Da, whatever, okay? So Lester picks up the horn and he says, Ba da doo bee bop, and he hit him over the head with the yardstick; he said, 'I played it wrong. I knew you weren't reading!'
So I think that was a pretty funny happening.
In Chilton's book, in writing about Lester, he mentions Boots and he says Sports, but Jimmy said it was Sport and not Sports. Is that it?
Yeah, it was Cousin Sport and Cousin Boots.
And Boots' name was Austin Young and Sport's name was Isaiah Isai Young, is that right?
I have no idea. No, Jimmy would know. You know, Jimmy would know, but I wouldn't. I have no idea what it was.
And Jimmy Talbert is your nephew?
Yeah, Jimmy Talbert is my mephe, but he kind of dug in to those type things, because he wanted to know something about ... before "Roots" was made, he wanted to know about his roots, you know? So ...

And Jimmy said I also should ask you how you felt about Boots and Sports' influence on Lester. From what he said ... Jimmy said that it was his impression that Lester was very impressed with their performance and their playing, and he took something from them in to his own.
What do you think? Jimmy said he didn't know, but he said thought you would know.

Well, unlike Jimmy, I don't really know too much about that. I always saw them as adversaries, you know? My recollection of it is because it seems to me that Lester felt as though, and rightfully so, you know -- he proved that he was right -- that he was much better, and Cousin Sport or Cousin Boots, whichever one it was, they tried to hold him back, you know, he didn't feel as though ... but

that could be because of his zeal as a young person, you know, and so I don't know. Maybe they were helping him and in his young mind, he may have thought they were trying to hold him back, you know, as the saying goes --but I don't really think so. I think, if anything, I would probably lean towards what Jimmy was saying, but anyone who picked up a saxophone, you know ... Lester wanted some of it, as the saying goes -- you know, he really wanted to see who was the better man; it would be just like a prize fighter or a wrestler.
At what age did he start feeling that way?

Well, I was saying - this was very young. He was wearing short pants, and I imagine that ... I can't remember, but it seems to me, I don't think he was more than 12 years old. I really don't. He was 12 or 13 maybe. When he challenged my cousin, you know, he wanted to battle him on the saxophone, you know? And that was just the thing ... and I don't know where he got it from, but that's the way he felt about it.

So that was -- they played in the saxophone family, as I'm telling you about, but it wasn't 3 -- it was 7. From Albuquerque, I guess we went to Phoenix, Arizona on the way to California and so we stopped in Phoenix, and we used to play -- and I started playing drums again, you know.
Oh, I left something out. Lester played drums first, you know?
Yeah, I know he did.

Did you know that? Yeah, he played drums first, and the only guy I've ever seen in my life -- he was an individualistic person more than anyone I've known, I think. You know how he held his horn up in the air and how he turned the mouthpiece around.
I was gonna ask you, why?
I have no idea. He was away from us then. I don't know ...
He didn't start playing like that?

No. When I saw him, that's what he was doing. I have no idea why he was holding it up in the air or upside down and that. But maybe it was things to come when he was a kid playing drums. Everyone would hold the drumstick between their forefinger and their thumb, because that's the way you're taught to hold a drumstick.

Well, he didn't do that. He held it between his forefinger and his middle finger. He didn't play anything with the thumb at all, and that's the way he held his drumsticks. But he held the left hand conventional - forefinger and the thumb. But the other, he held it between his forefinger and his middle finger. That's the way he held the drumstick. I have never seen anyone, you know, as long as I played drums after that, I never did see anyone ever do that.
So if he had stayed with the drums instead of the saxophone, he still would have had a uniqueness about him, you know.
Your father taught him drums?
Yeah, uh huh. My dad taught me drums, also. He taught all instruments. He was an amazing man, you know. I didn't realize it until later.
Was Lester's first instrument the saxophone or drums?
Drums. My first one was saxophone.
And that was when you all played in the family band?
Yeah.
You mentioned that your mother played saxophone?
Yeah, she played baritone saxophone.
Your mother played baritone?
Uh huh.
And which kind of saxophone did you play?

I played soprano first. And then I started playing alto, and then I played C Melody. You know, I went through everything, as I told you, you know. I've fooled with the trumpet, you know, the trombone, or whatever. The only thing I'm sorry that I really didn't --

he wanted me to play piano so badly, you know, and I just didn't want to fool with the piano at all, you know, which you just don't know any better, you know? That's the instrument you really should play, because he tried to get all of us to start on piano, you know, and I can tinker with it, as all of us can, but not to really -- the only one who turned out to be a pianist in the family was my niece, Martha Young, who is up in San Francisco, you know?
And that is Irma's daughter?
Uh huh. And she can play quite well.
She plays professionally, is that right?
Uh huh.
You mentioned that your mother played baritone sax -- what was her musical background?

My mother didn't have much of a musical background, just as I think I said earlier -- you couldn't live in the house if you didn't play something, you know, so my dad taught her to play baritone saxophone, you know, she just learned how to play her parts, but I mean, she didn't excell with an instrument.
What was her name?
Her name was Sarah.
S-a-r-a-h?
Uh huh.
What was her maiden name?
Now that's a tough question -- I really don't know; I don't remember that.
When your parents separated, you were 2? Is that right?
I think I was 3 or 3 1/2. Yeah.
And then your father married again, didn't he?
Uh huh. This is the mother I'm speaking of; the one that played saxophone, who was Sarah, who was my stepmother.
Oh.

Who was really the only mother I really knew. Because if someone rears you from the time that you're 3 1/2 until you're an adult, that's the only parent you know, so she was really a wonderful lady, and I say that, you know, don't like to talk about her too much, because she was, really, you know, dear to me. You know? So ... but he really made a good choice -- I don't know about his first choice, but I know his second choice was really a gas.
What was your natural mother's name?

Gray. Her name was Lizetta. Now she was from Louisiana and very fair, and creole type person, you know. I never did see her after I left, when I was 3 1/2. I guess like 1921 ... I don't think I saw her any more until
like, 1941 or '42. That was the first time I'd seen her, you know? So it's kind of, I guess that happens in a lot of families, so that's ...
Lizetta -- was that L-i-z-e-t-t-a, or L-i-s?
No, L-i-z-e-t-t-a. Lizetta. Gray. I remember her name.
Your father and Sarah were married where? In Minneapolis or in New Orleans?
No, I think -- and I'm saying I think -- I think it was Tippeydill, Louisiana. Have you ever heard of Tippeydill?
I think I have.
Yeah, this is what I think ... I think they were in Tippeydill, Louisiana. Yeah, see, that's an area that you know, I would be kind of guessing in that.
You mentioned the carnival and the minstrel shows. What do you remember about them? The whole shows?
Oh, well, I remember the minstrel shows, you know, like you're a kid and they had the 'Midway' -- if you're not a country girl, you may not know about the Midway.
Well, I lived in Oklahoma for a few years when I was a child.

Well, we played Oklahoma. And they had -- you know, you'd be at this carnival and they had flat cars where they carry the tents and the things on this, and they had all kinds of shows, they had the minstrel shows, which was really a big attraction, and they had side-shows like with the freaks in the circus, and they had -- what did they call those things? I forget the name of these stands they had where you spin the wheel, and you know, and they had the Ferris Wheel and the Merry Go Round -- well, all this was with the carnival when the carnival came to town. They'd put up the a Ferris Wheel. And they would have as many people out seeing them put the Ferris wheel and as they would who put the Merry Go Round together than you would see the people who attended. They had where you would win prizes from knocking bottles over and the cupie dolls and all that, and you'd spin a wheel of numbers where you could win things on. And you know? Those carnival people were really, really together, because you go into a lot of places and the roughnecks in the cities that you'd go in would try to destroy certain things, you know, on the Midway? And they had a saying that I never will forget, when a fight was about to occur, they would holler, 'Hey Rube!' -- and when they hollered 'Hey Rube' guys would jump from over the stands and drop their horns and run to the fight. That meant that the rube in
that town had started something; these guys had started something and the guys at the carnival would come out and swing with at everything, you know.

So as a kid, you know, you'd see that. And they used to have a Wild West Show; the thing that I remember, when we would go over to -- when I would go and try to see the Wild West, they used to have - they had a little jackass that the kids, the little kids would ride, and if you could stay on him for a minute, you know, he would get a prize. Between our shows, I would run over there every show and try to ride this jackass and he would throw me off every time, you know?
So that's just some of the fun things you did.
Was it mostly fun?
Oh, yeah, it was for me.
For a child?

Oh yeah, for a kid, yeah. You'd find ways to make different - to earn money in the show, and I'd go and get a bucket of water, you know, can you imagine getting a bucket of water and getting a dime for it? That was my little hustle, or whatever it was, but yeah, the carnival life, it's really a great life for a child because it's just fun and games to you.
At the time, you're getting quite an education, too, see? Because I think by the time I was 13, I'd been to
Gee.
Right. Been to almost every state in the Union. And so it is an education. You don't realize it and you know, you don't realize it a lot of times, but it is.
Did the carnival go east, too?
Oh, yeah ... the carnival went all over.
But I mean the one you traveled on.

The one I was with went mostly in the south, you know? It's a funny thing. The people, as I said before, it's like the circuses; you go to winter quarters --they called them winter quarters, you know, and they don't come out until a certain time of the year -- I think it's the Spring when they came out. But like the carnival we were with, they had -- they would play the same places every year and there's another carnival that would take place -- the other one would take, maybe the midwest,and we would take the south and another the north. I don't know ... but you know, those were fun years in my growing up, so I think what I'll do now is try to come back over to Phoenix and see if I can ...
But may I ask you something else first before you get to Phoenix?
Okay.
About the Minstrel shows, what were they like? What happened?

Well, Minstrel shows were one big tent. They were tent shows -- tent minstrel shows, and there was a large tent, like, not as big as the Big Top with the circus, you know, but it was a big tent, and I think it would seat, like, 3 or 400 people, and that's a lot.

But what you would do if you played county fairs or something, you would do like, 4 or 5 shows a day -- or 5, 6 shows a day, you know, however many people were on the midway, and if the midway was really crowded, now they may not get but a 15 minute show, you know, and they may get more, but that's with the carnival -- but you're asking about the minstrel show?

Now the minstrel show was a full performance at all times, and that was where -- and it seems to me that Ida Cox or somebody was on a minstrel show that we were on -- and they used to; it seems to me we played Baltimore, Maryland. I don't know why -- well, I know why that sticks in my mind, because, you know, as a kid certain things stick out in your mind, and Baltimore stuck out because the houses looked alike because the steps, you know, in Baltimore, the steps are right on the sidewalk, and that's why I remember we did play Baltimore with -- you know, you have something to identify with when you're a kid, and it would be some things that maybe

an adult wouldn't identify with, but when you've been to all these different cities and all of a sudden you come upon a city and the steps are on the sidewalk, you know, you know that really looks odd to you.

But the minstrel shows, they would have like, maybe 10 or 12 acts, and they would put on a 2 or 3 hour show, with intermission. And they used to sell the programs and they would sell photographs, that's really the thing you do -- you sell your act -- would try to sell your photographs. And you sell them coming in the show; now you wouldn't sell too many when the show would start, but at the end of the show, the acts that they really loved, they really would buy the photographs.
You know, in later years after I was with Nat, we played -- who's the woman who did "Some of These Days"? Sophie Tucker?
Uh huh.
Sophie Tucker was on the beach with us in Miami -- that was about in 1956 maybe, and she was selling her book after the show. So show business doesn't really change that much, you know?
Uh huh.
She'd never sold her books before the show, and so I was telling the guys that that's what we used to do when I was a kid, and she was sitting right out there, but
they loved her show, see, and now they were gonna buy it, you know.
You said the various acts -- were they all different or were they similar. Did somebody sing and somebody dance and another was music and another was comedy, or what?

Yeah, well, they always had comics, you know, because it was slapstick comedy, you know. But they had a lot of acts that were similar, but it's who was the best, and the business -- you will hear people talk now about shows and who wants to open and who wants to close the show, you know? But when you come up in show business like on TOBA, well, one thing you learn, we had -- my dad's act featured Irma, Lester and I, you know.

I forgot to tell you that they also sang and danced. Now that was probably the trio they probably were referring to. But it wasn't saxophone. Lester, Irma and myself -- you know, all three of us danced and sang, and so I think maybe that's the reference that they have. All of them did, yeah.

And we were -- what you don't do on the show is ever follow kids, you know. You don't follow kids and dog acts, that's what they always said, you know -- you don't follow a kid act or a dog act, and so my dad used to always say, who's gonna close the show? Well, he would say, we'll open it, you know? We'll open it. Until they could not get

on stage, you know -- not when the kids got out there and started singing and dancing and jumping all over the place. And even if you had a certain amount of talent, the other acts just couldn't get on stage. And they used to throw you money, while you were dancing on stage.

And when I was doing comedy, I had a way that every time somebody would throw a quarter, I would make the music stop, you know? My mother used to laugh, and so I would say "Hold it" and then I would do a dance and do a step and pick up the money, you know.
But that's the years that was were -- that's just show business, I guess.
Did that stopping and holding it, did that get more people to throw money?
Oh yeah, always. Always. It's called "milking the audience".
Did you get to keep the money?
Oh no! No, you know, those were rough times, so I didn't get a chance to do that.
Was this an all black carnival troop or just the minstrel show?

Nope, just the minstrel show. Just the minstrel show -- but on carnival, everything was white but the show that we were in, you know, and it was all black -- it was a minstrel show, that's what it was called.
And you know, like they had -- well, they're

really not called banners. Something else ... I forget the proper word for them, but like you see the lady -- this cut up, and it would say the "Sword Lady" and all of that, and they gonna put her in the box and they used to put my sister in the box and put the swords all through there, you know.
Ooo!
But it's just a gimmick, you know -- the box is made so you can ...
How does it work?

Well, I don't know -- all I know is that she guides them through to the next one, and guides it through the next one after that, and you just can't imagine someone being in there, but someone figured it out scientifically where you don't ...
Well, your sister must know.
Oh sure, she knew how, you know. But those shows were kind of gimmicky, you know -- it was a lot of false things in those side shows. There really were.
So should we go to Phoenix now?
All right, we can go to Phoenix now.

Okay. We'll get back to the music. Well, as I think I stated, I started playing drums then in Phoenix, and we had the band. We used to play at a place called West Lake Park. And I think we used to play there 3

nights a week, and that's when Lester left. Lester left and went back to Kansas City, I think, because he -- Lester was not a kid that you could chastise away like you could me. You know, parents learn -- or they should learn -- that you cannot treat, if you have 3 or 4 kids, you cannot deal with all of them in the same manner, you know. They all have different temperaments.

And I recognized that after I was grown, that Lester just -- you could not whip him with a belt, because he must have run away from home 10 or 12 times, you know? Because any time my dad would take off his belt and whip Lester, he would split. He was gone.

And I remember one time in the south, he ran off to someplace in Oklahoma, and we were getting ready to go back to Minneapolis, and I don't think they'd seen him for 7 or 8 weeks, and my dad had just gone up to the window to buy the tickets for us to go back to Minneapolis, you know? And my mother was just crying because she was gonna leave Lester there - - and hadn't seen him in ages, and my dad went up tothe window and says, you know, "Give me two halves and two wholes" -- those were tickets, you know -- you'd buy them in half fare, you know?
And so my mother said to my daddy to look around, and Lester was standing over by the door, and he said, "Make that 3 halves."
How old was Lester then?

I don't know ... he was a young cat. He wasn't -- he had to be very young, because we were going back to Minneapolis, right? That's what I said. And in Minneapolis, when I left Minneapolis, I was in the 4th grade, so it was during that time when he was very young. But he would run away if you hit him. But I wouldn't, you know. They needed to beat me, you know? They didn't beat me enough.
Why do you say that?

Well, because I was stubborn, you know. I was very, very stubborn. You got to be stubborn if you get beat for the same thing 5 and 6 times. But that's what I was saying, Lester -- I think talking to him would have done it for him. Talking to me, though, wouldn't have done it for me. Never would have done it for me.
Did anyboy ever find out where he had been and how he had gotten by for 7 or 8 weeks?

No. I got to tell you. See, he was the apple of my daddy's eye, no question about that. He was the apple, but when he would come back, everything would be okay. He never did question him -- never questioned him. And you're talking about a time when men really would question their kids.
But being an educated man, I think it helped him not to really pursue it and start beating on him again; he

wouldn't even discuss it with him -- never did ask him. We never did know where Lester had been or what he had done. But that used to happen so many times -- when he would come back, it was like he'd never been away. He just picked up where he left off.

I asked you off the tape when we paused a few moments ago, if your father tried to change Lester's position with the drums when he held the drumsticks in a different way, with his right hand, and you said no, that your father always recognized him as being an individual. What did you say?

I think so. Yeah, I think that he must've recognized that he was different and he wanted to be different, and don't think that I profess that I knew this at the time -- since this time, I've had kids of my own, and this is what I'm saying. I believe that he recognized that there was something about Lester -- maybe he wanted recognition, why he held the sticks differently; maybe he wanted him to say, 'Why don't you hold the sticks right?' You know, maybe he did and maybe he didn't -- but whatever it was, he knew he was holding them wrong, but he was holding them wrong and playing right!
You know? So which is -- where do you stop? I think that if you're a teacher, sometimes what's conventional to you is unconventional to someone else, you know? So I don't know.
Did your parents encourage individuality among the three of you, or ...

Well, I got to tell you. I have to believe that they did. You know, in retrospect, I would have to say they really did, because I'm pretty strong in that respect, you know - and mine is in another way; mine shows up another way. And I think Lester's was with his music and with his, you know, with his horn. Yes, I think that they -- and I don't know how, but I'm sure they did, because that's the way we all ended up, you know, because I'm very -- I'm overprincipled, I call it, you know? I am overprincipled. That's what I call it.

So I think they did -- I would have to say yes to that.
You mentioned briefly, sort of in passing, that you were a blackface comic --this was in connection with what? The minstrel shows?
Uh huh, and the carnivals. Yeah. My sister has a picture someplace; as a matter of fact, my son has a picture. I must have been around that tall.
That's about what? Three feet?

Maybe. And I was a black -- my face was black and I had a big bow tie; the bow tie was larger than I was; it was made out of paper -- it was like pink paper or something, and I had on a white sailor's cap, and
a little black coat. I don't know ... my son has a picture. He's kind of in to those things. I don't want to see them; I can't imagine anyone being a blackface comedian, you know.
And I told jokes, too. I used to ... yeah.
Do you remember any of the jokes?
Oh no, that was just all slapstick comedy, you know.
Did that happen often? A black performer in blackface? I've heard of it a few times, but who started it? Black or white performers? It started with white performers, didn't it?

Oh, I think so. You see, some of the biggest minstrel shows were white minstrel shows, and I used to see those. They had the interlocutor -- did you ever see a minstrel show? Did you ever see it in the movies?
I think I've only seen recreations on film. I don't think I've ever seen a real one.

Okay. Well, you see how they're in a semi-circle. A semi-circle, and they have the interlocutor -- and he's like the straight man. Now, the funniest people in the minstrel show, and it's just like the chorus girls, you know, how the chorus girls dance? The better dancers were always on the end -- on each end. That's so the one that came out first was the better one, and the one that went off last was the better dancer, and the same -- they had the same type

of situation with the minstrel shows. They would have 10 or 12 guys in this semi-circle, and the guy sitting to your left, which is the stage facing the audience, the guy sitting to the interlocker's right, which is stage left, he was always the funniest man, you know.

That one. And the first chair and the second chair were the real funny ones. On the right and on the left; they were the 4 top comics in the minstrel show. And so the interlocker would address most everything to them. They had all the better jokes. But now after you go beyond 2, then the jokes were not so funny, and the guys were not so funny, but some of those minstrel shows, you know, I saw some of the white minstrel shows with all the blackface comedians, and, yes, they were really, really clever. They were funny.

And on TOBA, all the black comics wore blackface. Oh yeah, all of the black comics wore blackface, you know. Your makeup was -- whatever the stuff was called, cork. You know, it was cork, and you used greasepaint, make your lips white, you know, white greasepaint. Oh yeah, I used to make myself up. You made up with your hands. That's the way you did it.

But those minstrel shows were really fantastic. Some good performers came out of them. As a matter of fact, I would venture a guess that Al Jolson really came out of a minstrel show; I bet he did come out of a minstrel show. If
you looked it up and tried to find out, because he was, you know, he was singing "Mammy" and all that, and to me, he reminded me of those blackface comedians that I saw as a kid. You know?
Uh huh.

And later on, which I haven't even gotten to, when I was working the studio? I had recorded all of his music -- what's the thing that the young man made the one picture, who played in The Jolson Story?
Yeah, Larry Parks.
Larry Parks? Yeah, I was at the staff at Columbia then when they did The Jolson Story. I did all the music.
Oh, really?
But that's another subject -- we haven't got into that.
Okay, we'll deal with it when we get there. One other thing; you said that you once saw Bill Robinson when he was traveling with the medicine show?
Yeah, the medicine show, that's right.
Do you remember what year and where? Do you remember how old you were?
No, see, that's the difficult thing about me. Now I can tell you about situations and incidents, you know, but I don't have a clue to the year then, and if you

bring it on up in to the years, most anything I'm telling you about, I will not be able to tell you the year, you know? I have never been in to that, and I've never been able to do that -- but I can tell you the situations and what happened.

Now somebody else will have to tell me what year it happened, unless you're gonna come up to the years where -- I think from Nat Cole on I would remember, you know, but beyond that, I couldn't tell you the year. Like I can tell you the year -- okay, we come from Phoenix and we come to Los Angeles, now do you want to do that? Okay.
Do you remember where it was? The medicine show?

No ... it was in the south someplace, though. Someplace in the south, because -- here's another thing that Bill Robinson did, and I'm sure that people that is in to him will know this. He used to do something which I saw him do as a kid, he would run backwards faster than most people could run forward. And he used to bet on it, and he used to win, you know? The guy was fantastic. You look that up sometimes, and see how Bill Robinson could run backwards faster than most people could run forward, and he won a lot of money betting on that. And he did, too. He could.
You danced before you played drums, right?
Well ... not really.
Or did you? You played drums before you danced? Do you feel there's a relation?
Oh yeah.
Between dancing and the drum playing?
Yeah, that's why it was so easy to pick up, you know. And Buddy Rich does the same thing, you know.
Well, Louie Bellson was a tap dancer.
Right, right.
Buddy Rich was a tap dancer.
Right.
Cal Tjader was a tap dancer.
Right.
And who else? There's 3 or 4 others, and I've heard an awful lot of drummers say that ...
Yeah, and Jo Jones danced, you know.
I don't believe I remember that.
Yeah ... but Jo danced. He'd get up in a minute and challenge you. And the recent drummers, I guess, too, in later years -- because they played so much for dancers-- and it is so closely related.
That's another story I'll tell you about -- that's how I got a job at MGM playing drums, because I could dance.
With ...
Do you remember "Strike Up the Band" with Mickey Rooney? That was why I got the job.
Was that your first studio job here?
No, that wasn't my first studio job here, but I think I better try to get to bring you up to that part, okay?
Okay. We'll go back, then.

Okay. When we left Phoenix and came to Los Angeles, as I told you -- Lester had split. Well, when we got to Los Angeles, then I did an audition because I was a better singer than I was a dancer; in fact, I could really sang. And now I'm thinking that I'm probably 13 ... let me see, yeah, I'm about 13 years old now.
When you got to Los Angeles?

Yeah, and so my dad took me -- they had a club here called the Apex Nightclub and at that nightclub, Ivey Anderson was working, Eddie Anderson, and his brother, and a guy named Gus Jones. They had a trio, and his name wasn't Rochester at the time -- I'm speaking of Rochester Anderson.
Eddie Anderson ... his brother -- what was his brother's name?
His brother was named Connie Anderson,

and I think the guy's name -- the big guy was named Gus Jones. And let's see -- there was a lady, Lottie Gee. Now if you go back and look and see about the Lafayette Players, I think this lady was from New York and her name was Lottie Gee. Just a marvelous voice she had -- she was a soprano. But Ivey was working there, and a woman called Mildred Washington who was producing the shows, and she had a sister that sang; her name was Flo Washington, okay?

So they had Guest Night at the Apex Club -- and so my dad took me and I went to the Apex. You know, at 13, I broke up the show. So the gentleman who had the Apex -- his name was Curtis Mosby -- did you know of Curtis Mosby?
Yes. Uh huh.
Okay, well Curtis Mosby owned the Apex club, and that was the biggest club ...
He owned it or he ran the band?
No.
I always thought he owned it, but ...

No, no. What I'm telling you about -- in later years, he had a band there, but when I'm speaking of now, this is 1929 or 1930, okay? When we came here, Curtis Mosby owned the Apex nightclub; it was the biggest nightclub in town. They were in competition with, I think, the Cotton Club in Culver City was running then -- Sebastian's Cotton Club - but I'm sure it was. But this was THE place. It's
really the old Club Alabam -- that was the Apex, right?
Right, yeah. Next to the ...
Right, next to the Dunbar Hotel. Okay?
Uh huh.

So they hired me, you know, he talked to my dad, and I go to work, and Rochester used to take me to the fights -- Eddie Anderson and I used to go to the fights every Tuesday night at the Olympic with him, and then we'd come to do the show. And my dad liked Eddie, so he would let me go to the fights with him.
But I did tell you that Ivy Anderson was in the show, that was before she joined Duke.
Uh huh.
And ...
Was there any law that said a 13 year old ...
Yes ... yes; I'm gonna get to that, okay?
Okay, fine.

So I was in school, and I met a guy that was going to Jefferson High School, and I was going to Lafayette Junior High School, and so because he was a real good dancer, and we had an assembly at Lafayette, and he came over from Jeff and he and I did a number together, you know? And I told Curtis Mosby about him, and then it was
all right; I'd gotten away with it. You know, but then the Labor Commission came down on the club and made me quit working, so that's ...
Because Curtis hired the other boy, too, right?
Yeah, so that bombed us out, you know, because I guess, you could get away with one, but not two, because of the child labor law in California was pretty strict.
So then I think that's when I really got in to music seriously when they made me stop working at the club.
You were working there as a singer and dancer?
Yeah, as a singer. Yes.
And a dancer, or just a singer?
No, I was just singing. You know, and that was ...
And the other boy was a singer also?
No, he was a dancer.
Oh, he was a dancer.
But we would do a dance number together, you know.
Do you remember his name?
Yeah, his name was Jack Williams. Yeah.

His name was Jack Williams, and he later went to New York as a singer. Now he continued to dance, but he was one of the best at doing the Sam? You heard of the Sam? Well, he was great at that and the slides and all that; he was really something else.

But after that, then I think I really got in to music, you know, pretty heavy, and I started getting my child's life together, you know, playing basketball and playing baseball and doing all that, until I started really ... now we moved next door to the Musicians Union.
You were living on Central Avenue?
Yeah, Central Avenue. And ...
Central Avenue and what?

1706 -- between 17th and 18th on Central Avenue. And I had always heard, as I expressed earlier, that I had been to -- I only knew New Orleans like 3½ or something, you know, 3 years old. But I always heard how clannish the black people from Louisiana were, you know, they really were always together.

And it came up for Papa Mutt -- he had an audition that where he needed a drummer, you know, so all these drummers went over on West Pecos someplace -- it's over near Georgia Street, I remember, there was a club over there -- but that was where he was holding his audition. And about 4 drummers, they played, for him -- and here I come, you know,

I must have been 18 or something, you know -- and with all my hair cut so short, and he said to me, he said, "Hey boy, what's your name?" You know, and I said, "My name is Lee Young." "Lee Young? What's your father's name?" I said, "Professor Young." "Where's he from? Is that the Professor Young from New Orleans?" I said, "Yes" -- he said, "Can you play?" I said, "Yeah", and he sent everybody else on and gave me the job. He never even heard me play!
But because I was from Louisiana, he gave me the job. But the footnote to that -- he was right. I could [cure leather] for him! (PHONETIC)

So I worked with Papa Mutt for quite a little while, and then Buck Clayton -- Buck Clayton had a band; let's see ... Les Hyatt had a band at the Cotton Club, okay, and I'm coming up about 5 or 6 years later ...
Can I take you back to Papa Mutt?
Yeah, but I don't know too much about Papa Mutt, though.
How long did you work with him?

I don't have any idea, but I worked with him, I don't know, because he was a nice man, you know, and I really did like Papa Mutt, but I don't know how long I played with Papa Mutt because you have got to remember that I was much younger a musician, you know, and I was in to a different type of music, actually -- but I did pride myself
on playing whatever the job called for, you know, and I'll tell you a funny story of what I did when I got started in L.A.

You know, no one knew about me, see, and they had separate locals here -- 767 and 47. And 767, the black musicians, they worked 7 nights a week; all the jobs they worked, they worked 7 nights a week, with no night off, you know. In 47, they had one night off a week. So I found out where all the black bands were playing, and I chose 5 of them, and I went to the different places, and I told the drummers that were playing at those 5 places, because they were married, and I was living at home with my family; I wasn't married, and so I said, 'If you want a night off, if you want one night off a week, I'll work in your place on Monday, I'll work your place on Tuesday, and I won't charge you' -- and you know, I was playing for them free, and I promised I would never take their jobs, but I wanted the experience.
And so I got a chance to work with 5 different bands, playing 5 different types of shows, and I did that for about 4 or 5 months, and after that, that's when I got the job with Papa Mutt.
But you got to get started somewhere, you know.
Do you remember the 4 or 5 bands? Which bands they were?

I think a couple of them were in Long Beach, because the pier in Long Beach at the time was really, really popular, you know? And they had a couple of bands down in Long Beach and they had out in the Firestone district, out there, and ...

How big did the kitty get?

Oh yeah, the kitty would get bigger than the salary was, you know, because as I told you, I would work free for the guys but when we would get off, they had to split the kitty with me, so I would go home with $5 or $6
or $5.75 or $6.75, you know, but the kitty was always much larger than the salary, which they were working for.
Now, after that experience with them, I'm gonna try and be specific about the years which is always, as I told you, it's hard for me to do.

Okay. It seems to me right about this time was when Buck Clayton had formed a band called The Fourteen Gentlemen of Harlem, and Les Hylte was at the Cotton Club, and he had a drummer which was Lionel Hampton, which was with Les Hylte. But Buck Clayton had a drummer -- I got it -- his name was Baby Lewis; he was a left handed drummer, and he was a very, very smooth drummer, and I remember one night at the Apex Club, you know, after I had started playing music, they had a Battle of the Bands at the Apex Club, and Les Hylte brought his band in from Culver City, the Cotton Club, which was the big white club here and the Apex was the big black club.

And Buck Clayton was the younger new band coming up, and Les Hylte was pretty well established because he broadcasted every night on KHEJ, too, incidentally, twice a night, as a matter of fact -- used to listen to both broadcasts, and he had Lionel Hampton with him, and had a great trumpet player with him named Lloyd Reese -- I'm surayou must have heard of Lloyd Reese.
And Marshall Royal was in the band playing lead

alto; Marvin Johnson was playing third alto; that's when they were just using three saxaphones, and the tenor player was Chuck someone -- you know, I don't know, or remember him, but I do remember ... oh yeah, Henry Prince? Yeah, Henry Prince was the pianist, which was the bass player that was with Nat at first ... his name was Prince, Wesley Prince. Wesley Prince's brother.

This guy was playing piano with Les Hyte's band, and I was trying to remember the trombone player -- Sonny Gravin was the trombone player. See, the reason they're kind of rough is because in later years I got to know them better, you know, when I finally was accepted, and then I knew them better. But I was just trying to run down -- oh, and the bass player -- I don't know the bass player with Les's band, but that night, all the younger musicians thought that Buck Clayton's band cut Les Hyte's band, you know, but we were probably biased, because, you know, I don't think that Buck's band had been together too long, you know.

But anyway, it seems that Buck Clayton took his band to China. He got a job in Shanghai, China. The guys went to China, and they were stranded in China, the way I remember the story. Anyway, so I don't know whether the union or the musicians got together and didn't have a chance to send for them or what, but they were stranded over there.
But they were pretty nervy during that time, you
know, to even go over there.

Now speaking of Buck Clayton, when they returned to the mainland, some of the band disbanded, and then they got the band back together and they were going to work at a place called the Club Arabee -- the Club Arabee was out on 55th Street; there used to be a nightclub upstairs, and they had like, 12 chorus girls and they had a big show -- a very large show.

And so this was my first big band to work in, and the way the band was dressed, they wore pinstriped pants frock tail and long tail^coats, and ascots -- ascot ties and collars. So you know, they were the Fourteen Gentlemen from Harlem, and they were really, you know -- no one was really dressing like that in bands, so I think it was really kind of unique.

And so they wanted me to join the band, and so I'm the youngest guy in the band, and I was the teetotaler, and I didn't drink or smoke and I just hadn't been around people who did a lot of swearing, and in the band, as I remember, was Frank [Parsley.] Frank [Parsley] was a guitarist; really a good musician. The bass player's name was Jonsey. Before I joined the band, when they went overseas, Jonsey was playing tuba in the band, and then the tubas went out, and he had to learn to play a string bass, you know.
And I was trying to remember some of the other
musicians, but I guess being a young man, you're always impressed by the guy that really stays on you the most.

In this band, all these fellows were very good musicians -- and I never will forget that at rehearsal, we were taking something down, some arrangement Buck had made, and there was -- you know a dotted quarter or something; I probably played it as a straight quarter, and Frank [Paylsey] turned around and looked at me and said, "You little young S.O.B. -- read your music!" You know ... and I jumped up and said, "Nobody calls me an S.O.B.!" And all the band jumped up and said, "You 13 of them, so sit down and play your instrument!"
