Can you remember how old you were?

I think I must have been 19. Let's see ... the years always get me all screwed up. I think I must have been around 19 -- maybe 20, you know, but I was a kind of a mama's boy, so when you get out there, you don't like to hear that.

But I think that that was one of the good things that happened to me, as far as music was concerned, because they were good musicians, and Buck was a real good arranger, you know; a lot of people didn't know that Buck arranged, but Buck Clayton was a good arranger.
I don't know why. You know who was in the band? I just thought of this. Hershel Evans was in the band.
Gee!

That's right. Hershel Evans ... maybe you should look that up and see if Hershel Evans didn't play with Buck Clayton's band, when Buck Clayton had a band, because I remember when Hershel came to town, because I used to jam all the time and Hershel used to like to jam, and so I think that Hershel was in the band, wasn't he?
That's what it says here, in Chilton's book.
Well, what year was that?
Let's see -- with Buck Clayton's band in the Brownskin Review.
Well, okay.
But it doesn't give the year.
It doesn't mention the Club Arabee and doesn't give the year?
No.
Okay. Now I can take you to Paradise and all that; that came later though, see.
Well, it says joined Count Basie with Buck Clayton in autumn, 1936.
Yeah, they both left here to go join Basie ...
So all we know is it was before '36.
Then we must be talking about '35. That seems right, you know.
What was the Brownskin Review? That wasn't at the Arabee?
No, that wasn't at the Arabee. I know what that was; I'll get to that. I think I do.

All right, so after the Arabee, it seems the band broke up and like you mentioned, Charlie Echols. Charlie Echols was the west coast's Cab Calloway. Charles Echols. He used to get a lot of gigs -- but he always wanted the best musicians. He could not play a note, but he stood in front of the band like Cab and he would sing these songs and he would conduct the band and shake his head because he imitated Cab, really, but not -- he couldn't scat and all that, but I mean he was the west coast's Cab Calloway, and he was good for a lot of the musicians because he was a personality, and he got a lot of jobs for them and he had a lot of good musicians working in the band, you know.

I played with him much later, but you know, at this point in time, I didn't work with him yet, but it seems to me after Buck Clayton, I really started getting my recognition, you know, at Stuff Smith came out ... I know this is in '37-- Stuff Smith came out, oh, let's see ... no, I got to go back.
After Buck Clayton I think I must have gone with
Ethel Waters and Eddie Mallorgy. Okay, this is the first time I left home, really.
Okay, Tyree Glenn, Don Bvas and myself --now what's wrong with that -- the reason I'm ahead of the story is because, no, I'm not ahead of the story; it's okay. This is fine.

Tyree, Don Bvas and myself left with Eddie Mallorgy, who was Ethel Waters' husband, musical conductor, whatever -- it was the first time I was gonna leave home, and Tyree -- Tyree Glenn, I'm speaking of.
Uh huh.

I had to play for them to see if I could do it -- I had to like audition. Now there was a drummer, a real flashy drummer from New York and his name was Willie Jones, you know, a real flashy drummer, you know, he wasn't a school drummer. And that was during the era of the Lindy Hoppers.
And so they had Lindy Hoppers traveling with them, and they just wanted to know if I could play 4/4 as fast as they wanted to dance, and that's how I really got the gig there.
We left here and we went up to San Francisco, and we came back here, and my son's mother was my girlfriend at the time. She was from Kansas --City originally.
That was Louise Rankin.
Louise Rankin, yes. And as we came

back through town -- no, this is a little off -- Ethel Waters didn't allow me to ride the bus with the other musicians. No, I rode through ... well, she thought that they would sway me because I was the youngest guy in the band, so I rode through; she would put me in her car; it was a big Lincoln and I rode through the country with her chauffeur, so I didn't ride on the bus with the other musicians.

But anyway, when I came back through, I stopped at my girlfriend's house and I told her I was going to, you know, we were going on the way to her home. To open a theatre there. And so it was the oddest proposal, I guess; I said, "If you come to Kansas City, I'll marry you." Because that was her home, you know.

And we drove -- drove all across country to get to Kansas City to get there and so we got there and opened at the theatre, and I did get a wire that she was in town, and that's how I got married. Now, when I married her, I quit, and I only stayed with them for that week; I must have stayed with them for 3 weeks; 2 weeks up in San Francisco and then one week at the theatre in Kansas City, but the reason it wasn't as bad as it sounds, the other drummer stayed with us but all he was doing was sitting in the wings, watching me play every night, you know, but I had the gig.
But they had to take him back to New York, you see, because they couldn't leave him out here stranded. He
He was from New York. And so when I got married, I just went in and told Ms. Waters that I was homesick and I got married and I was going back home.
But I was homesick, too, because I'd never been away from home, and so I came back home and then ...
Was your wife in show business? Because I know that later on she was a showgirl, or was she dancing?

Yes, she was in show business because I met her when I was working, and she used to work at the Cotton Club at the time. And I used to meet her. So all the performers and musicians used to meet at a drugstore at 43rd and Central. You know, when you get off. We had clubs like the Bell Tavern and you know, the ... Topsys -- there was a place called Topsys out on Firestone Boulevard.
Did all of those places have music?

Every one of them. Yeah. They had so many clubs in Los Angeles that had music, you know, during those years, and a lot of them had -- they had piano players and vocalists or piano players and a drummer, you know, some of them, and the drummer would sing or the pianist would sing, and that's when people like Harvey Brooks and Walter Johnson ... I don't know if you've ever heard of Walter Johnson, the pianist, he used to work with a guy -- just the two of them, used to work all over Los Angeles -- just the piano

and a singer -- Johnny Horace. Johnny Horace was his name. They worked every club. L.A. was just loaded with musicians, and clubs and places to play, and really -- remind you, in later years of like, Philadelphia. You know. Los Angeles was what I am speaking of, in the thirties. There were jobs all over town. I don't even know if there were enough musicians to go around.

So anyway, right after this, Fats Waller, there was a place called the Brown Derby right here on Vine Street. The Brown Derby was where the musicians union is? The Brown Derby was right on the corner across from that carwash now, do you know where that is?
The 800 block of Vine Street? The Musicians Union is at 817.
Okay. Well, just -- it was on the corner. What's the name of that street? The Famous Door was -- it's the corner that is north of the Union?
Uh huh.
That's where the Famous Door was.
Oh. Uh huh.
Now the Famous Door was -- the comic that was on Bob Hope's show all the time with the big moustache?
Jerry Colona?
Jerry Colona. Jerry Colona was a musician.
Trombone.

Jerry Colon was a trombone player. Well, at the Famous Door, when I went to the Famous Door, well, Jerry Colon's brother owned the Famous Door and he was a red headed fellow; his name was Red something, they called him - I don't remember what his name was. But he brought Stuff Smith out, okay. Stuff Smith played the Famous Door -- the Famous Door was right there by the Union. Now this is 1937. The reason I know this is 1937 is because we followed him in there with Fats Waller. Fats Waller I followed ... I worked with Fats Waller when he came out here on the coast, right? But Stuff Smith had a band that just came to town and just you know, blew everybody away. That was Jonah Jones on trumpet, and Cozy Cole, and Clyde Hart on piano, and Stuff Smith playing violin. Now, I don't remember who was playing bass, but they had 5 pieces. And the place was packed. It was jammed. Every night. And every Sunday they would have a jam session. Every Sunday. See Los Angeles was known for jam sessions then, they used to have jam sessions all the time -- and I would go out and play every Sunday -- all the drummers, all the trumpet players, everybody would come in and they would jam. All afternoon -- Sunday afternoon, at the ... let's see. After they left ... well, let me go a little further.
Who all can you remember being there at the jam sessions?
Oh, at the jam sessions? Oh, every -- I don't know, but every musician that was in town at that time. They would be there, because that was the place to be Sunday afternoon, and ...
Were black patrons allowed to come to the Famous Door?

Now you see, that I don't really know, because I could, you know, being a musician, because I would go to work with Cozy Cole almost every night, and any drummer that could hold the stick I went to hear him play, you know, because I felt as though that I could learn as much from the bad drummers as I did from the good drummers. I learned things not to do, you know, not to become sloppy and not to get lazy and you know, have pride in your playing. But I learned so much from Cozy, because Cozy -- he was a practice freak. He lived at the Dunbar Hotel; I used to meet Cozy every morning at 11 o'clock with my practice pad and my drum guide, and we would go through -- we'd go through the book together.

See, Cozy was a rudimental drummer, you know, and so he was a stickler for rudiments. And I think that basically, he really did help me because I'm not sure if I would have been as good as reading if I had not spent hours and hours with Cozy, because that's all we would do - just stay in the book, stay in the book. All day. And we must have gone through

3 or 4 books while he was here. Then after they left then Fats Waller came out, and Al Morgan was here at the time. Al Morgan used to be bass player with Cab Calloway, so he had quit Cab Calloway here, and we became very good friends, and so he knew Fats from New York, and so Fats was looking for a drummer, and so the three of us were the Fats Waller trio at the Famous Door, you know.
What was it like working with Fats?

With Fats? It was ... you know, I really didn't know who I was working with. I had heard so much about him, but he made me very cognizant of the difference in pianists, you know. Because I played with a lot of pianists, and then we would have sessions on Sundays and it's really amazing how the same person can play an instrument like the piano and you can really tell the difference. You can tell the difference, and you know, it's amazing. It's almost like, I can't explain it, but it's just like if, well, I should be able to explain it, because it's just like a violinst, you know, a concert master opposed to a guy that's playing a B or C. You'll be able to tell it immediately, because I guess they just take charge, you know. But Fats is my son's Godfather, you know.
No, I didn't know.
Yeah, he was ... when I was working with Fats, that's when my son was born, and Fats was his Godfather.

As I told you, Al Morgan stayed out here. Well, Eddie Barefield also stayed out here. He left Cab. He jumped ship, as they would say, and you know, he formed a band out here and he had some of the best musicians in the city, and what we would do, he had no job, you know, no idea about getting a job, but the music was so good -- I'll never forget, Buddy Harper used to be the copyist, and he would copy all the music and Barefield was just turning it out -- we would go to rehearsal, and we would have at least three new arrangements every day, and who was it?
Did you know the Indian trombone player named Chief somebody? His name was Chief. *
No.

Well, in later years, he went -- no, we called him Papoose out here, that's what it was; that's what the story is -- he was Indian and he was rehearsing with Barefield's band also, and in later years when we saw him back east -- he went back east and started to play with all the bands, but out here we called him Papoose, and so when we run in to him in New York, the first time you'd see him, you'd say, 'Hey Papoose!' and he would say, 'I'm Chief back here, they call me Chief, they don't call me Papoose!'
So we used to rehearse at the Union ... no, this wasn't the Union. It was right across from Jefferson High School when Covan had his dancing school? Jefferson High

School, on 39th or 38th Street. This is where we used to rehearse with Eddie Barefield, okay. And Paul Howard was in the band. Jack McBea was in the band ... what was that guy's name? Dudley Brooks was playing piano, and who was bass? Gee ...
What did Paul Howard play?
Paul Howard played the tenor saxophone.
Uh huh.

So it was really a good band, and it was a musical education, really. You know, because you're out here and you're getting a chance to play these -- all these, you know, fantastic arrangements that you know, Barefield's been with Cab Calloway, and you know, we hadn't been to New York, and so it was just -- really a trip.

So I think after that, we did get a job, had a couple of jobs, a couple of three one nighters we played together, and I used to do all the singing with the band, you know. Because I was, as I told you earlier, that I was a singer first, and I used to do all the singing with the band, and we played Easter dances, and we played the big thing down in Santa Monica on the pier, what they used to have every year, and ...
What was the big thing at the end of the year.
Don Blas was in Barefield's band, because

I'll tell you what Don Byas -- we worked at the Cotton Club for a week or something while Les Hite was on the road or something, we replaced him, because Les Hite was a house band at the Cotton Club. And the thing sticks in my mind; the reason I remember Don Byas and this band was because we had different guys in the band that used to make charts, you know? And Don Byas made an arrangement on "Dinah" and he arranged it in a minor, and everybody used to play "Dinah" in up tempo, and he played "Dinah" slow, you know, like da ba da da dee ... you know, it was really slow, and it was, you know, in those days, they used to have, like -- saxophone choruses, you know, the whole saxophone section would play one chorus alone. And that's what he wrote it about.
Yeah, Don Byas was in that band.
How long had Don Byas spent out here?
Don Byas was out here quite a good while, and he went away and he came back, and then he went back east and he stayed. And then I think he went overseas. As I remember it, you know.
So after Eddie Barefield ... I was trying to think what did I do after that. What was that ... '37? Oh, we're getting up into, and yeah, my kid was born December of '37. Hold it a second.

Okay, after Barefield, I started gigging with different bands, and you know, around town. I'm trying to think when did Nat come out with the trio. Nat Cole was -- he came out; at first he was working alone as a pianist, right? Then he started the trio with Wesley Prince and Oscar Moore. They got a record date. They were supposed to record over at Decca - and Nat was really very good about everybody singing with the group.

So they wanted me to come with them because I could sing the solo. See, at the time, Nat did not realize that he could sing, you know. He was just singing things like "On the Sunny Side of the Street" -- and other things were intrumental, because we made a record for Decca called "THe Black Spider" -- I don't know if you ever heard of it, but it was an instrumental, and it went really, really fast.
And we did about 4 or 5 things at Decca on Melrose, I think -- I think Decca was on Melrose, right?
Uh huh.

Now during this time, now I'm working with him, you know, I'm working with him at these places where he is going to record. Now he got some kind of a job where you were making measured music, and I had bought a new set of drums. Do you know what 'measured music' was? It used to sit in drug stores, and cafes, they used to have, sitting in front of you, that told you what was on the juke box, right in front of you, if you sat in Thriftys or wherever it was --

they had this right in front of you and you would sit at the counter, and it was called 'measure/music' and if you put a penny in it, you'd get so much music; if you put a nickel in it, you'd get more. Right?
Uh huh.

Now Spike Jones had something to do with this. I had never met Spike Jones at the time, but he was doing something -- engineering or something, but he got Nat to come out, Nat and the trio plus myself to record some things for this measured music thing, because he was involved with it in some manner; I don't know how.

But I set up my drums; I had a brand new set of Levi drums, and I set up my drums, and he told Nat -- he said, "No, he shouldn't play drums on this; he shouldn't play drums. Tell him to take brushes and play on his case, you know, on his drum case."

And, like, I went crazy, you know? I got these new drums, and here is some kook in the booth talking about telling me to play on my drum case. And I wouldn't do it, you know, and I said I never heard of it, I wouldn't do it -- I'm gonna play my drums. So I ended up playing the drums, but later on when we, you know, in later years when I went with Nat, we used to discuss it that it was Spike Jones -- you know, he was really showing you then that he was in to sound effects.
Uh huh.

You know, you know what he ended up doing, anyway, making those little funny records he made, and he was quite successful with them. But I think that was what he was hearing then and he was trying to make me be a part of that, which, you know, wouldn't work.
Was this the first time Nat used drums?

Oh yes, I was the first drummer he had, yes. Now, I was working with him for awhile on the Swanee Inn, and I didn't work with him very long; it may have been a couple of weeks or something, and I got a call from Les Hyte. Now, this is what I was telling you about. Les Hyte had a drummer with him whose name was Pepe Prince. He was a cousin to the other Prince that you heard me speak of; Wesley and Henry Prince, I think it was.
So the Rum Boogie ... no, not Rum Boogie, but the Cubanola -- that was at Beverly and Labrea.
And the Swanee Inn was on Labrea, right?

Uh huh. And the Cubanola was just north of that, where there were some gas stations or something. But it was on the west side of the street, and the name was what it was -- the Cubanola -- it was, you know, the Cuban music and Latin music was quite in, then, and so I always had my drums in my car -- always in the back of my car, and so I

was sitting home practicing one day, and Marshall Royal called me one day and said, "Can you come out here immediately?" I said, "Well, what is it?" You know, and he says, "Well, I think you got the gig, because this music is rough and it don't look like anyone's gonna be able to make it but you, and so we got to have you for the gig."

And Les Hyte cut his band down to 8 or 9 pieces, and I think it was like 9 pieces, okay? And so I jumped in the car, you know, and you couldn't get there then like you can now, but to me, I got there FAST -- because I lived on 55th Street near Hooper, and I had to come to Beverly and Labrea. And I came in and played the music, and we opened that night, and that's how I started working with Les Hyte, and then Les Hyte went from there to a place called Omar's Dome. I don't know if anyone told you about that.
Uh unh.
Omar's Dome was on 5th and Hill. Hill? Yeah, 5th and Hill -- Omar's Dome. Really a plush club, downtown.
It's right by Are you talking about the new Philharmonic Auditorium.
Yes.
Yeah.
Yes, but across the street was where the red cars used to go in to the subway terminal, that's right.
Subway terminal we called it.

Well, Omar's Dome was across the street where they now have these little theatres or something, but that's where it was -- it was Omar's Dome, it was a beautiful club, and I don't know how long we worked there, but we broadcasted there, 3 or 4 times a week, you know, and again, I was singing "My Reverie" and all the love songs, all the ballads -- I did all the ballads with him, and after that, I think that should take us up to, let's see, did I miss anything?

Oh, yes I did. I left a big space out there. I was wondering what I was doing in '38 and '39 -- now I remember other things I was doing. Okay, my first studio job, okay -- my very first studio job was ... gee, it was at the Paramount. Paramount Studios called me, they had a young boy named Billy Lee, and he was in a movie with Fred MacMurray and Ozzie Nelson, his wife, her name was Harriet ...
Hilliard.
Harriet Hilliard. That was her name. And it was starring Fred MacMurray, and the name of the movie was "The Coconut Grove" and they made it at Paramount.

And the object of this was this little boy was supposed to be a drummer and he was supposed to play. He was about 7 years old. Billy Lee. And he was supposed to close the show or something, as a drummer -- and I had to
go out and teach him to play. But I recorded and taught him what he did -- and that was my first studio job.
You say you recorded, you mean it was your drumming on the soundtrack.

Yes, it was my drumming on the soundtrack. Yes. And the next studio job that I got, it was the same type of thing, and they were auditioning drummers to teach Mickey Rooney -- Judy Garland and Mickey Rooney and Paul Whiteman were all in a movie called "Strike Up the Band" -- okay? I think Busby Berkeley, as I recall, he was the producer. Busby Berkeley, or was it? No ... I think it was Bugby -- it was either Bugby Berkeley or Minnelli. Minnelli ended up being her husband, right?
Uh ... yeah. Right.

It was Busby. It was Busby Berkeley. It wasn't Vincent Minnelli, but I did work with him, too. Later. So they brought -- what was Johnny's name? The drummer that used to be with Scott -- Johnny Williams. Do you remember --the what Scott quintet?
Raymond?

Raymond Scott Quintet! Yeah, the drummer was named Johnny Williams, and he was supposed to be top. So they sent to New York to get him to do this, you know,but the trick in it, you know, you had to teach Mickey to play, you know, and there was a great drummer ... well,

Johnny couldn't do it because he couldn't teach Mickey, you know, and he had to play this whole thing. There was a great drummer on the staff over at Fox -- Twentieth Century Fox -- because that was when they had staff musicians, you know, and at this point I was not a staff musician, you know, I was just a freelance musician, and well, they tried him -- Dela Nova or something like that, an odd name.

But Georgie Stall used to come -- where I was playing; he had heard me, you know, Georgie Stall was kind of a jazz buff, and he made all of the rounds. And so he called me and told me I should come out and see if I couldn't get the gig, and so I went out to MGM the next day, and he met me at the gate, and they asked me -- I have to be honest -- I was really cocky at this point, you know, I was real cocky, because you know, I thought that I could just play anything, and I met with Georgie Stall and Alex Hyatt, his name was -- it's funny how all these names are coming to me -- he was head of the music department. So he took me over and introduced me to Mickey, and wanted to know if I thought I could teach him.

And so I asked Mickey, "Can you do a time step?" You know, now we were talking about dancing. I said, "Can you do a time step?" He says, "Yes, I can do a time step." So I say, "Can you do a break at the end of the time step?" And he said, "Yes." So I said, "Okay, break at the end of

the time step goes da da dee da da ..." He said, "Yes." I said, "Do it." And he did, and I said, "Okay, now take your hands and say da doo dot dot ..." And he took his hands and on the table and did the dat dee doo dot ...

And I took him over to the set of snare drums and I said, "Now do the same thing, but when you get to the last beat, hit that cymbal" -- you know, and I said, "Hold them you want." And he just held them wrong, of course, and he did the dot dee dott dott, crash, you know. And they hired me, you know, because I could teach him.
But that's where the dancing help ...
So it is true? You can tap dance and play the drums.

Oh yes. Yeah. I worked on the movie -- it seemed like for ages, because I started off -- when I started off working at MGM, I used to have to take the S car -- you know, the street car, and transfer to something else and they would put me off and then I would get the bus and then I would be in Culver City, right? But the reason I know I worked there so long was because I bought my mother a housefull of furniture, I bought my sister a car, and when I finished working on the movie, I was also driving a car, too. I had a car then. So ...
That must have been a long-time while.
Yeah, I had the run of the movie, and

then at that time, they were paying ... oh yes, there is a little thing you should know about this -- when I got ready to record it, as I told you, I was pretty cocky -- and I was always at the studio, like they didn't use the term 'black' then, you know, I was always the only 'colored' musician, as they said, there.

Now, when we got ready to do this thing, that's when they would ... it must have been like 4 or 5 pages of music, you know. But musically, I always had a fantastic memory, you know, almost photo-full of static -- if I could -- if I read it a couple or 3 times, you know, I really had it, and so this particular day, you know, this is when you record everything together on the big soundstage at MGM, and there must have been at least 45 musicians. And George Estolle sat me right in the middle of the men because it was a featured number, you know. So he sat me right me in the middle of the orchestra, and I had 2 music stands in front of me with these 5 pages, I think it was, of music, and so we went over it, and in the studios, you don't rehearse, you know. Let's go!

And so we started playing it ... we started playing it, and it was someone in the trombone section that kept goofing, you know, and it was at that time when they didn't say, "Let's take this 12 bars ..." and they would always play it in its entirely, and so if you made a mistake, you had to

stop and start all over again.
And I think that we must've stopped and started,
stopped and started, and we'd almost get there -- and we
wouldn't make it. And, so now I know it by heart. And it's
a funny thing, how you want attention? You know? I knew that
I was in another world, but I wanted to be accepted, and
I wanted everyone to know. And I know this is exactly why I
did it.

So, I took the music and I put it under my seat,
and I sat on it. And so now after they were doing all this
talking to the people in the booth and everything, getting
it straight, and they turned around, and he tapped on his
stand, and he says, "Well, let's go!" You know, and so I got
my sticks and I was ready. No music ... he sees no music, you
know, and he says, "C'mon, Lee, let's go!" I said, "I'm
ready." He says, "Well, where's your music?" I said, "I'm
sitting on it", you know, and he says, "Well, let's go," and
I said, "I know it. As many times as we played it, I know
it!"

And so he came with the downbeat, and I played it,
and after I played it, all the violin players tapped on their
stands like they do in legitimate you know, tick, tick, tick, like, you
know. But I was doing that to be noticed, you know -- to let
them know that I thought that I was good.
It worked.

Yeah, it worked. So after that, what happened -- now they had promised me -- which was a lot of money -- they promised me $500 to do the recording. Okay? That's where the rub was. We did this session, and that's when the scale was $33 for 3 hours. $33. And so I guess I got my check, and they paid me for two sessions; we did two sessions, you know -- $66, and I called up and I said, you know -- I said that I would do, I would put the drum thing on there for $500. I didn't get but $66.

And so he says, well, you know, you want to make a name for yourself around town -- he tried to con me, you know, and I was always kind of a word person, you know, if you break your word with me, I couldn't live with that. So I said, "Okay, we'll just see who's gonna teach Mickey what I was doing when you get ready to shoot." I says, "You won't find me." You know ...so he says, "No, no, you'll be all right -- you're a young man, and you just got a chance and everybody is really impressed with you, and you're gonna get a lot of work here."
I says, "I don't want any work -- if you promise me $500 and I get $66.
Who were you talking to?
I was talking to the Head of the music department, because that's who pays you off. Okay, so now it comes time to shoot, and they get to this part -- now

this is 2 or 3 weeks before they got to this part. I got no call. But I found out that they were getting ready to start shooting this part, and I knew that no one could teach him what I had played but me, because but maybe they couldn't teach him what they had played, you know?

So I left. Jimmy Blanton and I were very, very dear friends, and we went up to a place called Val Verdi, you know, and I told my mother that -- and my sister -- that if MGM tried to get me, don't tell them where I was, because I ...
Was that a resort area?

It was a resort, yes. And so we went up to Val Verdi and sure enough, now they were in trouble -- because they had these drum solos down there, and they didn't have anyone to show Mickey what was done. Okay, so this big black limo that they use in studios -- I'm sure you've seen them, you know -- here's a chauffeur and the Head of the music department out there looking for me. Yes.
Well, I think now I better go back to where we were when we ...
Let me ask you a question about Billy Berg's. Did the Trollville open while the one at Peco and La Cienega was still open, or was its successor then?
Yeah, that's right.
And then he went to Hollywood later on?

I'll tell you where he went. He went -- Billy Berg's went from Peco and La Cienega to Beverly near Fairfax. Then from there, he went to Hollywood Boulevard, and he called it Billy Berg's Swing Club. Then he came to the one on Vine, which was where Harry the Hipster, Gibson and Eddie Haywood and those people and Lady Day and those people appeared. Do you remember the one on Vine?
Yeah, I remember the one on Vine.
Well, that's down there by the Ranch Market or something, isn't it?
Dizzie can still recite the address -- the exact address of the place on Vine.
Right.
It was 13 something ...
Right. Well, that was that. But I guess the point I'm really trying to make is how much music really was in Los Angeles then, and a lot of people were not aware of it;
really not aware of it.
So I'll go back and see if I can get out of New York. I told you that we went back to the Cafe Society, okay?
Uh huh.

I think we were there 2 or 3 months or something, and my father -- you know, our father became very, very ill; well, and my mother and I were very, very close -- and so when she told me that they were not expecting my father to live, then I left the band and came home. But you know, there's one story in the Billy Berg that I have to tell you, at from the beginning.

As I told you, when they had the band outside, Lee and Lester Young -- Billy Berg's appearing. This was our opening night now, you know. So Lester is in the band now, and they got our little marquee such as it is there. Well, what happened was Ben Webster and Jimmy Blanton called me. Sonny Greer was ill, and Duke was opening at the -- what was that out on Firestone Boulevard -- was that called the Trianon Ballroom?
I'm not sure.

Yeah, I think so ... on Firestone Boulevard; this is where Duke was opening. That was the same night we were opening at Billy Berg's, and sometimes you feel ashamed telling these stories on yourself, but it happened, and it was a fact.
So Frog and Bear called me to -- and they said, "Look, Sonny Greer is not gonna make it tonight; you better come on

and open with us, because you know, you want to play with this big band." And everybody wanted to play with a big band, and everybody wanted to play with Duke Ellington, you know, so I had told them that it was my opening night, that my name was out front, Lee and Lester Young. I said, "I'm gonna go play with Duke tonight; you'll have to get another drummer." And he said, "What do you mean? You're the leader!"

I said, "I don't care. I may not ever get a chance to play with Duke in my life, and I'm not gonna give this up." You know, and I signed the contract with the man, but Billy Berg, you know, he was very fond of me, you know - he had to be, because he says, "You've got to be the craziest man in the world. How can you be the leader of the band and you're not gonna make your opening?" And I said, "There's no need talking about it; I'm going to go play with Duke tonight." I always wanted to know how he started the band, you know, number one -- it used to be a mystery to me, because I could stand in front of the band, and he didn't count off or nothing, you know.

You know how you start playing the piano, and all of a sudden, here comes the band - BANG, you know, and that was always a mystery to me, that I wanted solved. And so I said, "I'm gonna go play with him." And I left him, and I left him and I played the Trianon with Duke and them that night. Luckily, when I came back the next night, I still had a job, but you know, it was only because the man liked me. Because, you know, that was a little far out.
Yeah. Did you find out how Duke started the band?
Oh yes.
How did Duke start the band?

Oh, he started the band by playing -- you get the feel of it, you know, because he plays certain things. Blanton was cueing me at first, you know, but after you know, during the night when I was there, I knew exactly when to come in because it's a feel that he plays, you know, it's the way he on the keys he makes his runs, you know, and these runs that he's making -- well, certain runs, it can only be one tune that he's getting ready to play, you know? You know that.

So like, it's like dazzling you with footwork, but everybody knew what the key to it was, and it's just amazing how he could do it, you know, but they've been together for years, and I really enjoyed it. If they weren't gonna let us work anymore, I still would have made it; there was nothing that could have stopped me from playing in Duke's band that night. So in retrospect, it's kind of silly, but that's what you got to do if you feel that way about it.
Did you get your pay?
Oh, yeah. The pay I think was something like $17.50! Which was, you know ...
Who did you get to sub for you that night?
I don't know. I don't remember who they got, but they got someone.
They got someone then -- you didn't?

No, no. I was too busy; I had to go to rehearsal. Even if they had a big show, I had to go and rehearse the show. Oh no, I didn't go. That was up to ... You left it up to Billy Berg? That was the end of Billy Berg's?
That was the end of Billy Berg's?
Oh no, I'm sure that Lester and them got someone, but no, they would leave it to him.
When Lester came back here to town after you left Basie, did you -- did he -- was he any different than he was before? You hadn't seen him for how many years?

Oh no, I hadn't seen him -- no, he was very different tome because, you know, I hadn't seen him since I was quite a kid. No, he came back once before that. My dad was ill once when he was in Kansas City with Basie, and Basie's chauffeur and Basie's car, you know, Basie let Lester have the car with the chauffeur to come out and see my dad. Now, that was the first time I had seen Lester as an adult, you know.

And I was asleep upstairs, and my mother brought him upstairs, and she said to me, you know, Lester had a very high voice, you know, and my mother said, she touched me and woke me up and said, 'Lee, do you know who this is?' And I looked up, and I said, 'No, who is it?' And she said, 'This is Lester!' And Lester looked at me and he said, 'Oh, look at

how big he is!" I said, "Listen to his voice. He sounds like a girl!" That's what I woke up saying. You know, about your brother, I said, "He sounds like a girl", you know, with that high voice he had.
So that was the only time and he was here.
Was he here very long, or just ...

He stayed about 10 days I think, and he brought a dog with him, I think -- you know, he loved dogs. As you can see on my desk there, we really love dogs; love animals, and he brought a dog; he always had a dog, but he always gave them the darndest names. This dog he had, it was a Belgian police dog, all black, and his name was Tonics, you know, because he used to have a musical saying, "Get your tonics together", so he named this dog Tonics.
He always had strange names for them.
Did he have a dog on the road with Basie?

No, I don't think so. But they lived in Kansas City, see, and that was their headquarters. But he left the dog here with me, and when he was here, that's when I was saying our voices were so similar, even though I was trying to make fun of him. I didn't realize that my voice has the same timbre as his. The dog would think that I was Lester a lot of times, so he left this dog with me, and this dog tore up 3 suits and shirts, and I took the dog out, which

is Watts now, but there was nothing out there years and years ago; there was nothing out there but just trees and all that, and I took the dog way out there and let him loose, even though I loved dogs, I left him out of the car, and we never did see Tonics since.
And my mother would say, "What happened to Tonics?" And I would say, "I don't know. I have no idea what happened to him."
So after I came back from New York, my dad did pass, and that must've been like '42 or '43. Now who did I go to work with? Where did I go to work?
Were you just -- what? You left your band at the Cafe Society?
Uh huh. Yeah, and then ...
You came back here then. And you didn't ever go back to it?

No. They didn't keep it. They disbande. Yeah, I had to be with it because nobody was gonna take care of the business, and I was kind of business oriented, and I took care of it, but that was really the end of the band. We didn't ever fool with it again.

Bumps came back here and Red Callender Calendar came back, but Jimmy Rose was -- and while we were working incidentally, Clyde Hart worked with us, because Benny Goodman took, you know, as I said, Benny stole Jimmy Rowles, but Clyde Hart used to work with us when we were at the Cafe Society.
An interesting thing that one of the acts that worked with us at Cafe Society was the woman that made -- what was it, a "Star is Born"? Judy HolXiday?

Judy HolXiday was one of the acts in the show. I was trying to think of the name of the act -- they had the craziest acts in the world. You know, the Cafe Society would always be Meade Lux. Lewis, Pete Johnson, and some little new act, and then the band, which was us, you know.

And Judy HolXiday had an act -- something about the shoe, you know? And I have a picture of her in that -- but didn't realize until after I saw it in motion pictures, you know -- well Red Callender was the one that told me who it was at the time, and so we went back and looked at the pictures, and it was her.
What did she do? What was her act?

It was a comedy act. It was like 3 fellows and her and they would do takeoffs on -- they had parodies and those types of things where they would do takeoffs. But she was funny then, you know - - she was a funny lady.
But we worked downtown, you know, in the Village. We didn't work uptown. Let's see, when I came back, let's turn it off for a second.
(CUT)
Testing, testing. This is November the 10th?
That's right.

I was speaking of the Cafe Society. I think that you wanted some input on what I thought about Lester from the time that I had seen him when we were quite young in Minneapolis, when Frankie Tromberg Trombanger was his idol, what changes he may havemade?
Yeah, well, how he evolved from that point.

Well, what I have to say is -- when Lester came out to California, which I said, was at Billy Berg's -- he was like any other musician that -- we knew his reputation; we had heard his records, and there's a little funny story about that.

The first record I heard of Lester, when Lester was at Basie's, as I told you earlier, that Lester would run off from home quite frequently. Well, I heard the record for months before I ever knew it was my brother playing, you know? Because we never heard him out here, as he was in Kansas City with Basie. So when we knew it was him was when our father became ill, and I told you that he came out to visit him.

Well, that was the first time I really knew that was Lester playing on Basie's records. So he -- his style, I can't say about that; I don't know where he came up with it, because I was not around, you know, during that time, but

when he came to us, and joined the small group that I had, he was well established, he was well known, he made many, many records with Lady Day and Teddy Wilson, and he did a couple of things with Benny Goodman. Was it "Tippy Tippy Tin?" No, that was something else -- but he made something with Benny Goodman that was kind of a classic; it was -- he played a good solo on it, but you know, when he first came out here, you know how the West Coast and the East Coast was? I don't know if you were aware of that.

But the East Coast musicians -- they didn't know too much of what was happening on the West Coast, you know? And maybe it was because of the trains or the covered wagons or whatever we had at that time. But Bumps -- everyone felt as though Bumps Myers, the people here in town, which was the tenor player, would really blow Lester away, because they always had their favorites, but it took them about a couple of sessions to understand what he was about. Because he really came up with jamming, you know, in New York, like they used to do at Monroe's, the Uptown House, and other places in New York, where they really would have cutting contests.

Well, I don't know how to say it, but Lester to me -- I'll just tell you what I heard in his playing; I think that it was unfortunate and it came at an unfortunate time -- and I always wanted to go on record as saying this -- that I do believe that the man who was responsible for recording him in later days and later years after he left Basie, and he

was no longer with us and he was traveling with the Philharmonic, well, when he started recording with -- and I will say with Norman Granz -- I think the things that he was doing really were almost demeaning, because it did not show the scope of the man as a musician.
Uh huh.

Because the man that was recording him, he was into blues, you know, so he wanted you to play some B flat blues and because that was about what he could understand. But, to me, if you listen to any records where Lester played solos on ballads, he's a very melodic musician, and he was one of the very few jazz musicians that, if he were to play "These Foolish Things" or -- what were some of the other things he used to play? "Polka Dot and Moonbeams" -- he would, the first chorus, he would always play the melody, you know, then he would work around the melody, you know, when he would start his improvisation.

But I was in New York once, and Norman Granz was gonna do a session with him, and I told him, you know, I said, "I'd like for you to do one song on the session for me" and he says, "Well, what do you want me to do?" And so we went across from Birdland, there was a big music store right across the street from Birdland, so we went in there and started looking at sheet music, and I found a song that I wanted him to do.
I wanted him to do "Come Rain or Come Shine" --

because that was the way I had heard him, and I knew when he played with us, the most requests that Lester got was playing ballads, you know, such as "These Foolish Things" and "I Can't Get Started." There was one thing that he did with Lady Day -- oh, "The Man I Love" -- just a beautiful solo, but the type of solos that I'm speaking of that he did with the melodies, you always knew what he was playing.

And if you go back and get the records where he is doing, "These Foolish Things" and "Talk of the Town" and "Can't Get Started" -- the lay person would always know what he was playing, and I really think that's why he was so well known among the lay people, because I think they related to what he did, because they could understand; he didn't play over their heads. Like in later years, when bebop first came in, the people didn't know what the musicians were playing, you know, that was really just for musicians, you know, and even some of the musicians didn't understand it at the time.

But I really think that the guy really did play melodic, and he played beautifully, and I just don't think that -- if he ever had a chance to record with strings and that sort of thing, I think you would have seen what the guy could do, but I don't think he was really given a chance because he was recording, and someone was recording him that I thought was very narrow in his musical taste.
The way that he played around the melody

No. Well, now he didn't -- no, his music was not --it just happened that way. But his music was a very personal thing with him, and I really think that Lester played to please Lester. If you go back and hear some of the stories, which I had to read about, when he was replacing Coleman Hawkins with Fletcher Henderson's band, you know, and I think you can read some of the liner notes I read where he was saying that Fletcher's wife would try and get him to play like Coleman Hawkins.
Yeah and play him Coleman's records.

Yeah, playing Coleman's records -- so was never in to that, you know. He was an individual, and he was a stylist; you know, he set the style, and I think when people like that -- Louis -- Louis was a style setter, a trend setter, and I think that we've had many of them in the music business, and they are all individuals and you can't turn them around, because it's just meant to be I think.

But he -- I think my preference was to always hear him play the beautiful things, because you know, and I loved to hear him play in the harder keys, but just to play in B flat and you know, it makes the instrument sound the same; where can you go? You know, playing 8 bar blues --that's what they were playing, the 12 bar blues, or whatever they would play,
they'd try to mix them up, but still blues are blues.
Was his approach to improvisation similar at the time he left home, or ...
Well, no; I don't ...
Was he improvising then?

Oh yeah, he could always improvise, but at the time he executed an awful lot. He played an awful lot of fast things; as I mentioned earlier, Franie Trombert and Jimmy Dorsey and those people had things like the Bouncing Ball. Well, that was like running a lot of scales, and that's what he used to do. You know, he used to run all over the horn a lot, but I think when he went to the tenor -- and this is just my assumption; I don't have any way, we never discussed it, I imagine it maybe was a larger instrument and he felt as though it wouldn't sound right for him running up and down the tenor, because maybe he thought it was more mellow, I don't know -- but he did change considerably.

But Lester played the way he was; that's the way I think. He was a very softspoken man, and he was an extreme introvert. You know, he was extremely introverted. He was not out at all. Very few people knew him. I'm positive of that.
You mean he was always like that, even when he was very young?
As a child. Yes, as a child. But of all

the people that have written things about Lester, that I have read, I only know one that really captured him that made me, you know, as his brother, sitting down reading it, thinking that that person really got to Lester, got to know Lester -- and that was Ralph Gleason.

When Lester passed, Ralph Gleason, I read something that Ralph Gleason wrote about Lester, and I never have been able to read it again, you know, because if I read it, it really breaks me up. But he was one person that -- he sounded like Lester had told him everything that he said, because you know, Lester used a lot of slang and he had his own language -- and only the people that he really cared for, that he allowed them to understand him, you know?
I understand he used to say things that rhymed with what he really meant?
Uh huh. Yeah, he did. Well, he did, because he just ...
And that his friends knew what he meant by hearing the rhymes.
Yeah. Well, he would give out nicknames, but they were names ...
Do you remember any of them?
They were names of endearment, you know, like, well, you know about Lady Day; that's been stated many times that he gave her that name. I don't know, you know?

But like we had a little trumpet player, you know -- some little guys act like little men, and they become really to other guys, they would say, "He's a cute little man, isn't he?" Well, Paul Campbell was a little fellow, and Lester used to call him "Ripty Gipty", so you know, I guess he would come up with many things that way.

About his playing, I think that -- I'm only sorry that he really didn't get a chance to express himself. More than he did. I'll tell you what he would do at sessions. He loved to play jam sessions, and loved to not know the tune. You know? And during the sessions, a lot of times, if you were playing a tune, the instrumentalist -- the soloist -- didn't know, well, it was fashionable for the pianist to turn around and say, E flat, 7th, you know, D flat, C Major -- he wouldn't want that. If he didn't know the tune, he'd say, "Don't call the chords to me. Just play the chords and I'll play." And I'd seen him do it many a time, you know; they just started playing, and he didn't know it, but he would play it -- but he would say it confines you too much if you know it's a D flat 7, you know, you start thinking of the only notes that will go in that chord, and he would say that's not what he would hear. He wanted to play other things and make it fit.
And he did. And I think most of the great musicians could do that, you know? So that's what that was all about.
You were saying about Bumps Myers and
Lester -- was there any more to that story? You said that when Lester came out, you said that everybody thought Bumps could cut him?

Oh well, the only part about the rest of the story is I guess, that it was just absurd -- didn't anyone realize how absurd it was until they played together, because, as I told you what he did about his cousin, you know, he would have to establish that he was the President. It was a good name for him, really, because you know, he kind of lived up to it.
Now I think we can id better leave New York and come back here.
All right.
Okay,when ... my recollection of '42 is; oh, I didn't tell you about '40. Before we went there, I showed you a wire a moment ago from David [Brokeman.]
Yes.
That was at CBS. That was a radio show that -- I don't know what the radio show was about, but I know Rafael Mendez was the featured instrumentalist. Are you familiar with Rafael Mendez?
No.
Okay. Well, he's a great trumpet player, and I think what we were playing on this show was the "Flight of the Bumble Bee" -- and they had a very, you know; in retrospect,

just thinking about this thing, I didn't think I would remember this, but the "Flight of the Bumble Bee" -- what always amazed me about doing this with Rafael Mendez and David Brokeman was the name of the conductor -- they had a bass player here in town that played tuba, and he worked at all the studios, and he was the best tuba man in town.

His name was George [Buget], and the way "The Flight of the Bumble Bee" was opened, everyone knew that Rafael Mendez was going to play it, but they started off with the tuba player playing the introduction. And so the tuba player played about the first 4 or 8 bars, you know -- 8 bars of "The Flight of the Bumble Bee" which was an introduction to Rafael Mendez.

So I guess the thing that always blew my mind about it was if you were awed by Rafael Mendez playing "The Flight of the Bumble Bee" on trumpet, I was so amazed to play a tuba player play "The Flight of the Bumble Bee" -- I never thought they should have let him play it, because it took something away, as far as I was concerned, you know, because the instrument is so much tougher.

And he played "The Flight of the Bumble Bee" -- he would play the first 8 bars, you know, and then, of course, Rafael would play it in its entirety, which, you know, he was established, and he was really a virtuoso. He was.
So I had a very good experiences playing with people of that caliber. Then I started freelancing in the studios,

and did a lot of things with Manny Klein. As a matter of fact, at the time, Manny Kline and Rafael Mendez were on the staff at MGM; they had staff musicians then, and Johnny Greene was there and George Estolle was there, and Lena Horne's -- which was not her husband at the time, but was to later become her husband -- Lenny Hayden. Lenny Hayden was on the staff, and MGM really had a great staff of musicians over there, and they had about the best staffed orchestra in town.
Was it unusual for a black musician to be working in the studios?
Well, I was the only one. You know?
I know. But this comes later. We're not to that yet.

We're not, right. But that was at Columbia. I did freelancing. Yes, I was the only black musician there. You see, the reason -- one of the reasons, which is another story which I'll tell you -- that we had separate locals here. I don't know if I explained that to you or not. We had Local 47, which is the Local we have now, and we had Local 767.

Well, I lived next door to that local, you know, as a kid, and I think I told you about the jam sessions and all that. But there was a thing that happened -- well, that's when I was freelancing, and I did a lot of studio things. I did, like in my scrapbook here, you'll see there's a thing I did with Hazel Scott, Red Calendar and I played with Hazel Scott

in a picture with Red Skelton called "I Doed It" -- and we did some things with Lena Horne; quite a few things over at MGM. And the Nichols Brothers were in some of them, but other than recording, I used to always at MGM play for the dancers.

I did a lot of Fred Astaire's things. And Phil Moore, well, before Phil Moore -- it was Calvin Jackson. Calvin Jackson was the only black musician working the studios, and he was working at MGM as a composer and arranger, but he didn't get credit for composing. As the man says, "Now it can be told" -- you know -- he would only show up on the screen credits as the arranger. They would not give him composer credits at the time.

And after Calvin -- Calvin was out there during the time I was freelancing, but I worked all over town. I worked -- I remember the first time the Delta Rhythm Boys came out, they worked at Hal Roach studios, and I know, they called me to Hal Roach and I went over and I recorded with them. I worked at Hal Roach, I worked at 20th Century, and Hindoff -- Ray [Hindoff] at Warner Brothers; I think that was where Ray Hindoff worked. Now Ray Hindoff did an awful lot for black musicians during those years, because he was really in to jazz, and at the Cotton Club, when Jimmy Luntzwood came out, Ray Hindoff used to be there every night, and Hindoff got Luntzwood to do some things at Warners with him -- I don't remember what ... was that where "Blues in the Night" was made or something?
I don't know.

Anyway, he had him to do something. And then I got to the place at MGM, and I was working there so much and they -- you know, I had made a pretty good reputation, and then they wanted -- they said they wanted a good trumpet player, a good saxophone player, a good trombone player, as they would say, a "colored" guy, you know.

So I started -- I remember that Luntzwood and Basie was in town, I took -- as a matter of fact, I took Marshall Royal to the studio, you know, because Marshall Royal was an excellent musician and he could read everything they could put up there, so that's what you had to do at the studio.

It was not how much you could improvise -- they only needed that once in awhile -- they would want a trumpet player, you know, to play some high notes like Pops, but you had to read the parts. That was the important thing. And you couldn't take all day to do it, you know. You had to read it down the first time.

So, that was my bag, and that's why I'm sure that I got in to it, but eventually I started bringing in a trumpet player, a trombone player, a saxophone player, at their request, and they'd tell me what type they wanted, and so I would bring them in. But I think somewhere in there, you'll find that Ray Hindoff was really in to a lot of jazz, and he -- will that be on here? Well, turn it off ...
So if you check that, you may find out something

on Ray Hindoff, because I think that he was instrumental somehow in getting people to Warners, you know, the different bands -- especially Jimmy Lunceford's band. I still -- it seems to me they did something over there -- the entire band, at Warners, for Ray Hindoff, so that was his name.

So I organized another little band that I had around town like 5 pieces, but in the midst of that, I got a call one day, one morning, early to come out to do the Camel Caravan -- it was the Camel Caravan Show -- right out here at CBS on Sunset Boulevard.

So I took my drums -- I loaded them up, I always loaded them up, so I ran out here and I set up. And we rehearsed, and we stayed all day and you did the show at 6 o'clock. And everybody was saying, you know, 'Hey, it's really great, and we gonna ... welcome to the band' -- and you know, we did 13 weeks of it.
Oh, I went home happy because I had broken the barrier. Then I go back -- it seems to me it was on a Friday -- I go back next Friday and I get set up, and there's another set of drums there.

And that really didn't bother me because when they left, they were talking about maybe I would have to play a solo on the show the following week, so it didn't really ring a bell. But when I get in, when I got in, rather, the contractor called me over and said to me, 'What are you

doing here, Lee?" And I told him I'd come to do the date. And he says, "But I didn't call you." Isaid, "I know, but you called me last week and you told me that I was hired after the show" -- and he said, "Well, you must be mistaken."

Now that was quite embarrassing, and the musicians in the band, you know, they started it -- they told me I should take it to the Board and someone in the band called DownBeat Magazine -- you know, at the time, that was the music magazine and was quite popular -- and so ... where is that thing?
It's here.
Let me get that date. It was in '43.
Who was the conductor?

Freddie Fisher was his name. It came out in the DownBeat, May 1, 1943 in big red letters across the top of it, in bold type, it says "Color loses Lee Young's job" -- then it goes on to tell you, you know, what transpired, but I think one of the reasons a thing like that could happen at the time was because of the separation of the locals.

I think earlier I had told you that the white local, they worked 6 days a week, you know, and that the black local, they worked 7 days a week; that's when I was coming up and I would let drummers get off and I'd work in their place for free -- well, what happened with this, there was a rule in Los Angeles that any transfer musician that came in to L.A. -- and I think that was a national rule, too; it may have been a

difference in the amount of time you had to put your transfer in -- but in Los Angeles, it was pretty stringent because you -- if you were from out of town and you put your transfer in, and you were not allowed to take a steady job for 6 months. Remember I told you that Lester had to sit outside on a box?
Uh huh.

Well, that was because of that law. Now, the black local did enforce that, because I told you that was enforced on Lester, but now, here was a case where I'll tell you who the drummer was -- when I went back to see CBS that next Friday, the drummer was Nick Fatool, and now Nick Fatool had been out here like 5 days.
Oh?

Yeah, because he had just left Benny. He left Benny Goodman and he come out, and had not been in town over 5 days, and if it would have been 5 weeks, it would have been wrong.
