They were gamblers and they were hustlers, but it's something about them as far as the black people were concerned, they always seemed to help the youth more than the more educated people.

Now I guess you could say that was because they had it rougher and they knew they wanted to improve -- they didn't want the kids to have the same type of life that they had. That's what I always attributed it to, because I know that I would have to go to a place like Fontana and Black Dot would pick up some of the boys at 8 o'clock in the morning, and he'd been out all night and he would sleep in the car, while we were playing baseball, you know, but the professional people, they didn't seem to do that, so I was just trying to equate that with what my dad went through.
Uh huh.
You know, many, many years prior to that, so I guess I'm saying I don't know how much we have improved.
You said your father's middle name was Handy. Was that a family name or was that indicative of a relationship to any other Handy's we may have heard of?
No, I don't think so. His name was Willis Handy Young, and Lester's name was Lester Willis Young.
Oh, it was Willis? Not William?
No, William Handy ... my dad was William Handy, and Lester was Willis, though. Is that correct? I think so.
Well, that's what I've read.
Yeah, that's right. He was Willis.
How about the Handy -- do you know where that came from?
No, I have no idea. I don't have a clue to the Handy. You're thinking of W.C.?
Yeah, well I wonder.
I don't really know. I don't really know. I wouldn't have a clue to that one.

Your father had a band in New Orleans. I read in Whitney Balliett's book, 'Such Sweet Thunder' that Red Allen mentioned his father; he said that his father and your father worked together in New Orleans.
Is that a fact?
Yeah.
No, I never read that -- I wasn't aware
of that, but maybe that's why when I met Red Allen, he was so friendly with me. He knew something I didn't. But no, I didn't know that. I wasn't aware of that.
Yeah, he told Whitney Balliett they played -- his father and your father played music together in New Orleans.
Well, they probably did, because you know, my dad was quite a good musician, you know.
Did Clarence Williams go to school at New Orleans University, or did he work with your dad's band or what?

Well, that's what I don't quite understand. See, all I know is that from the time it seems that I can remember, when he was talking about musicians, he would always say Big Head Clarence, you know, he said he was one of my prize pupils and he said that he left and went to New York and became very successful. But he was the guy that he used to talk about, you know, most when I was very small.

Now that's, you know, Cootie and Ben came much later, but this was the man who, when I was very, very small I would hear him talk about. Clarence Williams. And I've always wondered if the young man that was on television -- Clarence Williams the Third, that was -- I forget the name of the show where they had the one black and the white girl and the white boy -- not the Rookies, it was something -- it
was a good show out here, and his name was Clarence Williams the Third. I always wondered if he was any relation. I never got a chance to meet him to ask him.
You mentioned a great long string of instruments that your father played, but you never mentioned drums. Was that just an omission, or ...
Well, that was an omission, because I saw him play drums, too.
I figured that -- well, he taught you, right?
Yeah, uh huh. But I saw him play drums, too.
Okay. Do you know of any of the people who were in your father's band? I mean do you remember any names?

No. See ... no. Because the thing, the band that I think that was probably the best band was in Minneapolis, where he had a chance to go on the Orpheum circuit, I think, but he had 11 pieces and they were gonna take the band and myself, you know, in front of the band, and Lester and Irma.

But they wanted him to cut 2 men out of the band, you know, and he was a high principled man and he would not. And everybody was just dying to get on the Orpheum circuit, you know, that was the biggest thing that you could do in

Vaudeville then. But he wouldn't -- I remember that he would not cut 2 guys from the band, and so they continued to do those little one nighters up in Bismarck, North Dakota, you know, Devils Lake -- they used to play all over the Dakotas, but I don't think there were any 'name' people that we would know, you know, up in Minneapolis way.
Up in Minneapolis, you mentioned briefly the Pettiford family, and Oscar being a friend of yours, or was he a friend of Lester's?
No. Oscar, it seems to me -- no, not mine at the time. I met Oscar later on, but when we were in Minneapolis, no, I just know that I used to hear Lester talk about the Pettifords.
I understand they had a family band, too.
They did, yeah, but I'm sure that Lester was older than Oscar, because I met Oscar later on when I was playing, but I think he had some brothers or something; they did have a family band.
There was 11 children. I looked the Pettifords up after you mentioned him.
Yes, they did have a family band, because I know Lester used to -- I don't know which one he used to hang out with, but they used to hang out all the time.
But there wasn't any interaction of
any kind between your family band and their family band. You didn't play in any of the same places, or anything.
No ... not that I recall, no.
Can you trace your family back further than your own parents? Your own father?

No, I can't. Yeah, wait a second now. Okay ... gee, this is tough. There was a time when; it seems I remember when I was 3 or 4 -- I don't think I was even 5 years old that I'm talking about now, that I remember my grandmother, you know. My grandfather was a blacksmith, okay, and my grandmother was an Evangelist.
These are your father's parents?

Yes, my father's mother, you know, she was an Evangelist, and my grandfather was a blacksmith, because my daddy used to talk about how hard he used to work so he could go to college, you know, and my grandmother --I just remember her -- I think maybe I saw her once or twice, in a place called Natalbany (PHONETIC) Louisiana, if that's the way you pronounce that. I understand that's not 100 miles from New Orleans -- but all I can remember, it sounds like to me it was called Natalbany where they just had a store -- you know how in the small towns where they just have a commissary or whatever they call them. That's all they had, was just the one store where you bought everything; you know, all of your supplies for whatever.
But my auntie and my uncle and my grandmother and
grandfather lived there, so that's ...
Do you know how to spell the name of that town?
No. I can't even pronounce it! It's probably wrong.
Well, we'll look it up. What were their names?

Well, I'll tell you what it was near. It was near Hammond, Louisiana - Natallbany was right next to Hammond, and I know how to spell Hammond. I don't really know, though, because I, like, visit them from New Orleans to Natallbenny, and I went back, but I don't remember -- I just recall seeing them once or twice. They had a farm; they lived on a farm, you know.
Did your father and Sarah have children?
No. No.
Jimmy Talbert, whom we mentioned earlier, how is he your nephew?
Well, see, now -- I would have to say to you that my father was a traveling musician! Okay?
I see.
Talbert's mother is my half sister.
Because as long as I've known Jimmy, which is a long time, he always talks about Uncle Lee.
Oh, yeah, that's true. As I told you before, people from Louisiana are rather clannish, and so when I heard that I had these 2 nephews -- Jimmy has a brother.
Oh, I never met his brother.
Yeah ...
I know his sister, Lucille.
Yeah, but his brother is in Washington, D.C. He's an engineer or something like that. But, you know ...
I know Jimmy's from New Orleans.
Right.
All right. You mentioned that your sister Irma's daughter's name is Martha.
Yes, Martha.
And she plays professionally?
Yes, she does.
Tell me about her. Where does she play, how does she play -- classical music or jazz, or ...
Up in San Francisco ... no, she plays jazz.
Oh?
Yeah, she sent me a writeup not too long ago from San Francisco, and she sent me a tape, I've got to be honest with you, you know -- I was really pleasantly

surprised, because I had no idea that she really played the way she does. You know, she sounds really good; she knows what she is doing, and I called her and told her that I was really surprised and that I had no idea she could play like that. But she can play.
What -- does she appear in San Francisco?
In San Francisco, yeah. She told me the name of the club -- there are a couple of clubs she works in.
As a single?

Yeah, and a bass player; she plays with a bass player. She worked with -- I'll tell you who --they came up together. Alton Redd's daughter -- Vivian, what's her name, Reed? The girl who plays saxophone?
VY Redd.
VY Redd. Yeah. Well, she and VY Redd used to work together all the time.
Oh?
All the time.
Where?
When they were both in Los Angeles. All over L.A. And I think VY Redd appeared at the -- I think she was -- was VY at the Monterey Jazz Festival one year?
Yeah, I think so.
Well, Martha was playing with her.
Oh.

Uh huh, yeah, she appeared with her, but she is a surprisingly good pianist; she doesn't really play like -- generally, you can put me in one room and let somebody play the piano in another room, and I could tell if it was a woman playing, you know, and that's not to be a chauvinist, but you can. But it's the difference in the touch, you know. But ... you can't tell that with her, she's so strong. She plays strong piano. She really attacks it, you know.
Because even like Marylou -- Marylou played fine, but she was so dainty and so sweet with it, you know ... well, she was.
How old is Martha about?
Martha must be about 39 -- about 39.
Oh, the carnival that you traveled with was Lightman and ...
No, Lackman ...
Lackman. When I played the tape back, I wasn't sure what the word was. What was it?
It's Lackman. Lackman and Carson.
L-a-c-h, I think.
C-h-m-a-n.
Yeah, I think so. Yeah.
Okay, that was a word I wasn't sure of.
And you mentioned Ida Cox, and I found in looking her up, that she toured with White and Clark's minstrels.
Well, I imagine so.
Is that a minstrel ...
Well, see, I remember her as minstrel -- I remember her with minstrel shows, and I don't remember ...
You don't remember which ones?

No, you never do. But see, when you're that young, somehow you catalog these things and you do remember them, you know. And I don't know if I told you about -- there was a team -- someone would remember -- on one of the minstrel shows we were on, the man's name was Blind Denslow, and now I never thought I would ever remember his name again, but just in talking to you -- he was a blind man that performed on stage, you know, and he used to break the show up. And his wife would have to lead him to the wings, you know, and he'd go out on stage, and he was a singer and a dancer, and then, you know, she would call and he would go back in to the wings.
That's pretty unusual. I've never heard of a blind dancer.
Oh yeah.
Were there others?
No, I haven't heard of any others, but he did, because I remember his name was Denslow -- it's an
odd name, but he was on that minstrel show, the one that I said that we were on around Baltimore, when I saw those steps and things.
Uh huh. You mentioned that you and Lester and Irma danced and sang, and you mentioned that you were doing comedy; did Lester and Irma also do comedy, or was that strictly for you?
No, that was me. Lester would always be the straight man, you know, and I was the comedian because I was, I guess, more of a flake. It would be termed now, you know?
Did Irma give up music for good?
Yes, she did. Uh huh.
And that was fairly young, wasn't it? When you went to Los Angeles, right?
Right. Yeah, she didn't play any more, and then she started dancing and singing and she worked quite a few places.

For instance, when we first came here after I told you about the Apex, and then after I stopped doing that and I started playing music, she used to work downtown at the Burbank Theatre; there was a Burbank Theatre down here on Main Street -- you know, Los Angeles really had a lot of places for people to work in entertainment. That was because, for years and years, now that I recall --the
Follies downtown, there was some black bandleader here; he had the band at the Follies for years, and the Follies was an all white show, and they had this black orchestra in the pit.
And I'm talking about like 1932 and '33, I guess, you know -- '34.
But as late as the - what was it, about 1950, one of the white girls that was dancing down there got fired for speaking to one of the black musicians in the orchestra.
Oh, you're kidding?
No, because I knew the girl. And she knew Paul Kelsh, and she had a conversation with him, you know, like, 'Nice day' or something, and she got fired for speaking to Paul.
Yeah, well that shows you how unpredictable it ...
How old was Lester when he left home? I don't think we really established that. Or, do you remember exactly?
I wouldn't remember exactly, because I would have to discern when was the first time he left home.
Well, for good.
No, well, not for good.
Well, if you remember how old he
was when he first took off ...
No, he ... see, as I stated earlier, Lester used to run off every time my dad would raise a belt to him.
What would he do to upset your father?

Well, my father was a very strict man, you know, and he lived by the Golden Rule -- that it doesn't have to be -- that if you did anything that he told you not to do, you know, you would have to go and get "Greasy Jim" -- that was the name of his razor strap, you know. Well, I would go and get it and just stand up there and really take mine, but you couldn't do that to Lester -- because he would leave home.
I would say that the first time Lester left home, he was probably 11 or 12 years old when he run off from home.
And then when he left for good, he was about how old?

Oh, he must have been' around 18; I don't think he was any older than that, but he left for good -- the last time I think he ran off was in Salina, Kansas. Salina, Kansas -- and the reason I can remember that was because we'd been to Dodge City, and I'd seen some football games, high school football games in Dodge City. And Hill City -- I think there is a Hill City in Kansas, also, and we were playing all
around there, Topeka and Lawrence and all those little places.
About Papa Mutt. I know you worked for him just briefly here.
Yeah.

But I read in the Chilton book that he worked in the studios sometimes playing background music for, I guess, in the silent pictures, but did you ever do any studio work with his band, I mean, get in to the studios to play, whether it was for sound ...

Okay, let me tell you what that was, what they were doing then. You used to go to a lot of films, and you would see black musicians on the bandstand, but that was when you were working as extras, you know, you really don't play the instrument, you know, you're just part of the scenery, and if you see a nightclub and you see where there was a black orchestra.

No, they didn't make the recording, you know. I think that was a thing where the musicians were getting -- it was $33 per session, per 3 hour session at the time, you know, and so I think it was for stand-ins, as they called them. That's what they called them. They would get $11 or $12 a day.
Oh, I did a lot of those, too. You know, before I got my recognition and started recording.
Did you do some of those with Papa Mutt?

Not with Papa Mutt, no. But I did a thing with ... it seems to me, the Nichols Brothers when they were kids, they were in a thing, I don't remember the name of the picture -- with Nancy Carroll and Earl Dancer, really, was producing this cabaret scene, I remember that, because Earl Dancer -- I don't know, do you know of Earl Dancer?
Tell us about Earl Dancer. I've run to remember his name, yeah.
Yeah, he was ...
And I met him once.

He was Ethel Waters' husband at one time, and he was a producer, and he was quite good. He came from New York; he came out here, I understand, at the time, this was years ago -- this was in '30 something, that they allowed him to really direct this cabaret scene in this motion picture with Nancy Carroll, and it was a thing where the Mills Brothers -- not the Mills Brothers, I'm sorry -- it was the Nichols Brothers were in it, and I don't remember the title of it, but that was a long time ago.

When we were talking about the Club Arabee, I looked up something, and ran in to the name Brownskin Review, and you said on the tape earlier, 'I'll tell you about that later earlier.' And we never got back to it. What was the Brownskin Review?
I don't think it was the Brownskin Review.

I think it was the Brownskin Models. That's the show that I remember -- it was the Brownskin Models, and the Brownskin Models -- oh gosh, if I could only think of this lady's name; a beautiful woman; beautiful brown skinned woman, and she had all these beautiful brown skinned girls with her; she didn't have what you call high yellows and she didn't have the real black girls -- they were just what the name implied; brown skinned models -- and they all looked like models, and they were all beautiful.

But it's terrible I can't think of the lady's -- almost called it out -- she had this show for years, and she was from back east, and it was the first time they had migrated to the west, and they had some pretty bad times out west at first, but I can't think of her name. It's the Brown-skin Models, though, if you can look that up someplace, you'll find out.
And they were what? Showgirls?
Uh huh ... yeah.
They participated in the show as beautiful showgirls?
Yeah, but they danced, though; they didn't just parade like models would. Oh no. They were dancers and singers and they had quite a good show. I played for their show.
Oh, really? With whom?
Uh ...
With what band?

I'll tell you who -- it's a funny thing; I almost thought of it. As a matter of fact, that's how Callender Red Calendar came out here. Red Calendar came out here from the east with the show called the Brownskin Models, and he was married to one of the girls in the show. So the first time I saw him, he was up north appearing with the Brownskin Models up in San Francisco. You look that up on Red, and see if he tells that.
Okay. When you got out here, what did your father do? Did he have a band out here? Or did he play in a band out here?

No. See, now by the time we got here, what he did, you're talking about the WPA time now, okay? That's around '30,'31,'32 -- whatever year that was -- they had the WPA, but they also had WPA bands, and so over at one of the playgrounds, and he conducted -- the 22nd Street playground -- the band would meet there every day and they would rehearse I don't know how many hours, but they had to put in their time to get their WPA check.

But he conducted the WPA band when he got here, and also by the time we got here, there was an age involved then, also, because the musicians were young -- the same way they are now, you know? Musician passed 35, in jazz, if you just come in to a new town, you have a terrible time getting

started -- and he was older than 35, you know, and so that's why he had to go back in to teaching music, and what he did, was he conducted the WPA band and he used to give music lessons, and that was during the time that a lot of kids came up here in town that he taught, but I don't think many of them followed it -- because he was the type of person that -- he didn't get paid for all of the music lessons, like, he wouldn't even charge them, and the people in the neighborhood had kids, he would get them the instrument and they would buy the instruments.
As a matter of fact, Mike Gould was working in the biggest music store downtown, and that's where my dad used to get most of his instruments from, was from Mike Gould.
Oh? So Mike Gould really goes back with your family.
Yeah, well, we went to a track meet -- didn't I tell you that?
I know you had a message from Mike Gould here the other day about a recording.

Yeah, well, we went to a track meet one afternoon at the Colliseum and Mike Gould was sitting up there with us and he says, "Do you know that I've known 4 generations of this?" And so my son and my grandson and I were together, and he knew my dad, see? And so that's quite odd; I didn't realize it.
How old is your grandson?
Oh. That's Lee Jr.'s son?
Uh huh.
What's his name?
Mark. Mark 3. Whatever.
Does Lee have any other children?
No, he doesn't -- no.
And you have Lee Junior and a daughter; what is her name?
Roslyn.
Okay. The WPA band -- was that a jazz band then?

No, they played band music, you know, and like they tried to play -- well, I shouldn't say they tried to play, but you know, I was a young musician then and to me, that's just what I would have told you. That's what their music sounded like; they sounded like they were trying to play, but I mean, they were probably borderline musicians, you know, and the guys that he had to teach, a lot of them to play -- but it was a way, I think of giving people money then, to keep them off the streets, you know, because the other guys had to, like some guys had to dig ditches or whatever it was for the WPA, and during that time in Griffith Park, a lot of them were working in there and they had this big fire, and a lot of them were lost in this fire. WPA workers.
Oh?

Yeah. So the WPA -- like the CCC camp or whatever; that's what it was; to try to -- I think it was a program to keep the people off the streets. And so they had it for music, and they had it for the arts; you know, the theatre also.

Yeah. Back to Ben, you mentioned also that you met him in Albuquerque, and in the Chilton book, under Ben's name, it says that he joined the Young Family Campbell Kirkie Band in Campbellquerque, New Mexico and toured with the band for 3 months, is that right?
Campbell Kirkie? Campbellquerque?
Cam -- it says, hey, he must mean ...
He means Albuquerque.
He must not have understood what Campbell Kirkie somebody had said, because he wrote Campbellquerque, and that doesn't sound right.
I don't think there's such a place. It's Albuquerque.
I - I didn't say it out loud though.
It was Albuquerque.
Yeah. Okay. And he toured with your band for a few months.
Uh huh. Yes, he has those facts right. Yeah.
That's funny. If I hadn't said it out loud ...
Campbell Kirkie Campbellquerque.
Right.
Two words.
Yeah.
When you were with Charlie Echols, was it the same time that Don Byas was with Charlie Echols?
Uh huh, yeah -- I think so.
Well, then that was 1936 according to Chilton again.
Right.
And when you were talking about The Famous Door on Vine Street, you started out talking about the Brown Derby, and ...
No, I got them mixed up.
Okay, I just wanted to get that straight.
No, no. I didn't mean the Brown Derby, no.
So you didn't mean the Brown Derby; you meant The Famous Door
No, I thought I did that. No, they never did, no. It was The Famous Door.

Okay. And there was a reference to Earl Dancer under Buck Clayton and Chilton said that Buck Clayton, during the early 30's worked in the L.A. bands led by the Irving Brothers. Is that a name you recognize?
Yeah, but I can't remember them. But it seems like there was some brothers -- yeah. You read
that someplace, huh?
Yeah, in the Chilton book.

Yeah, there were some Irving Brothers, but ... yeah, they were early, though. Yeah, they were. It seems like one played guitar and another one played bad piano. I think ... I don't know. But yeah, I remember the names -- but I think this was a little bit before I got out there.
And then the next name it lists is Ellighew. Duke Ellighue. Was there such a band in Los Angeles?

Duke Ellighue? No. It could have been, but see, to me, it would have made more sense now that you said that, I just thought of ... see, when like before I got here, you know, we got here in 1929 and I don't remember any of those bands. It could have been during that time that I was in school, like from '29 to '33 that I may have lost contact with those people.

But I remember when I first came here, in '29, the guy that they were talking about most, his name was Rebb Spikes. That's the guy that seemed to have had -- and Jack McVea's dad was getting all the gigs, the banjo player. But that Ellighew, I don't remember hearing that.
Lavern Floyd?
Uh huh, yeah. Uh huh. Yeah, I heard that one.
And then it says Charlie Echols and
Earl Dancer. In 1934, when Clayton became the leader of Dancer's 14 piece band.

That was right. I'm sure that was Earl Dancer's band at first. But there's a lady -- they make no reference to Edith Turnham? Floyd Turnham's mother -- there's an Edith Turnham, she played piano and she had a band, and her son played with the band.
We did not find any Turnham in that book.
You didn't? Well, no, she had a band in Los Angeles at one time, and she used to have some good jobs.
What did she play?
She played piano, and her son was a very good lead alto player. His name was Floyd Turnham. Now he ended up playing with Les Hyte in later years.
Is that T-u-r-n-h-a-m?
Uh huh. Yes.
How big a band?
She used to have like 10 or 11 I think.
And that was what? Early 30's?
Uh huh.
You mentioned you went to Lafayette Jr. High School, but you didn't mention what high school you went to.
Polytechnic at Polytech and Washington and Graham.
Okay. Did they have a music program there?

Oh, yeah. Certainly they did. Everything I did -- and I think that musically, in junior high school it was better for me for music than high school, actually, because that's where I learned to conduct, really, in junior high school.

Because I had a teacher, her name was Ms. Goodrich, and she was a wonderful lady and a good musician, and she made me get involved in everything in junior high school, you know, musically? That was when I was in the glee club and I was in the dramatic class; I played Penrod and Penrod and Sam, and she was quite -- she had quite an influence on me, because she went to Jefferson High School. She transferred and went to Jefferson High School, and when I finished Lafayette, I went to Jefferson High School at first, and I really think I went there because, you know, Mrs. Goodrich was there.

That was an experience that I didn't realize, you know, because in later years, when I started conducting for Nat, it finally dawned on me, you know, why I picked it up so fast. I had forgotten that I had done it, you know, because we played all legitimate music in junior high school. You know, you played all the semi classics, you know, kind of heavy music you played ... symphony. And she used to --

whatever she would happen to be doing, I would take the baton and I would conduct the band, and when you're that age, you don't really realize what you're doing -- especially if you're a percussionist, you know, you don't really realize what you're really doing. Not what you're really doing -- I guess I'm trying to say how important it is; what it may mean later on.

And when I started conducting for Nat, it was really a simple thing, and the guys thought that I had been conducting for ages, but I had not. And then again, I had worked under so many good conductors, you know -- I worked under both Bachalegnakoffs, you know, I worked under Morris Stoloff, I worked under a guy at Warner Brothers, Ray Heinrichk, George Estolle, Johnny Greene, by the time I was with Nat, I had worked under all these people -- Johnny Greene and George Estolle, and Phil Moore was not bad, either.
He did some conducting at RKO Studios when he would make the arrangements. Were you aware of that?
No, I did not know that.

You know, Phil Moore did the movie at RKO for Fred Astaire -- that's where the song, 'One More for The Road' came from? 11 One for my baby, and one for the road, 11 when he was dancing on the bar and kicking over the glasses?
Uh huh.
Well, Phil Moore did all the music for that, and I played all the drums for that.
Oh?
Yeah. So that was with Constantine Bachaleynokoff; that was the other one. The other was Misha; the one that I spoke to you about.
The one you mentioned before, yeah. You also mentioned that you had done a film with Freddie Fisher before you had the Camel Caravan experience. What was the film you did for him, do you remember?

No, I don't recall what the name of that one was, because you see, that was at the time I was doing a lot of freelancing, and when you do a film during that time, I was specializing, too, you know, because they would call me because they had the legitimate drummers, and most of the musical things that I was doing --and it's just like any other record date, you know; you may not have a clue to the name of the movie you're going in to; as a matter of fact, you don't even care)-- because you just go in and they got the music up on the stand, and you set up and play and you try to get it to another date -- you try to make at least 2 dates a day, you know?

So I wouldn't really know the name of that picture, but I did a thing with Hazel Scott and Red Skelton called 'I Doed It' -- I was in I think Lena Horne's pictures, too, I was trying to think of -- I think it was 'Panama Hattie' -- was it 'Panama Hattie' or something?
I don't know.
Lena Horne was in it.
You also said that you would talk about working for Vincente Minnelli, because you ...

Well, Vincente Minnelli -- I was trying to recall, but I'm sure it was Busby Berkeley that did "Strike Up the Band" -- but Vincente Minnelli, what I did with him was some of the things that I did with Lena Horne. There was one thing that we did out there, I don't know what it was -- I can't remember what it was, but it was -- one of the featured things in it was about Jericho -- "Blowing Down the Walls of Jericho" or something; there was a trumpet player. I got him to do the thing. His name was Jack [Traner,] who was later with Lionel Hampton's first band when we left here.

That was a movie that Lena was in, and there was a big scene in there, you know. The big thing in town at the time with all the studios running were extras, you know. Whites and blacks got a lot of work from being extras. So they used to always have to go out to the casting thing.

Yes.

And we went to the doctor to have a checkup. And it was really a lark, because I never did go to a doctor -- and so we went up there for about 4 days, and when we came back, the nurse came and she got me, you know, and she says, "Mr. Blanton, the doctor wants to see you." You know. And I said, "I'm not Blanton -- he's Blanton." She said, "Oh, Mr. Blanton, he wants to see you." So he thought it was me, and this was when he had found a spot on Blanton, and really, we always really attributed that to -- because he perspired freely, and he used to play -- they used to play Chicago and New York in the dead of winter, you know, and Bear just -- you know, he didn't change clothes. I'll never forget, I picked Nat up one day at Adams & Hoover to go and see Blanton, and we got out there to see Blanton, and Blanton did not weigh 70 pounds then, you know, that's when we knew he was really going, when he was -- it was a terrible day for both of us, coming back.
