Nottingham?

Yeah, Jimmy Nottingham was in the Great Lakes band, Dudley Brooks was in the Great Lakes band, and out here at the Santa Anna air base, all the studio musicians were at Santa Anna air base, because I used to go out there and play with them all the time. But I think that he was railroaded because, maybe part of it was his fault, I don't know -- because I was working at the Downbeat here, and I took him downtown, down on 8th Street to be inducted, and he was inducted and went to Fort MacArthur, but that night he was sitting right in the front row when I opened up and started playing.

I said, 'What are you doing here?' And he said, 'I jumped the wall.' You know, and so he came over the wall and I took him back, and he went back over the wall and got back in camp, but it's a thing that he could not adjust to, you know? And I think that ... it's all past now, but I do think that it was unfair because he was a musician, and at the time, the caliber of musician that you were, then you did have a chance not to be -- but they put him in just the army,

just like any other buck private.
Sure, maybe I could have adjusted to it in all probability, but you're talking about a different type of person, you know? Joe Jones couldn't adjust to it, either. They had him in, you know, and he was a raving maniac, also. But most of the musicians I know did not have to carry that -- they didn't have to hack that, you know. But I think you're dealing with personalities when you get in to that, because it was his misfortune to probably get on the wrong track with whomever the officer was here at Fort MacArthur. And that's why they shipped him south.
But I will say this -- I never did understand this about the army. Most of the black guys, if they were from the East or of California, they always shipped them south. They did it -- to a man. They always shipped them south. And all the southern boys, they shipped them to the West Coast or the East Coast. I'm speaking of black soldiers. When they sould induct them in Georgia or Mississippi, they would ship them to California; they'd be stationed in California, in Illinois, or in New York or Jersey.
But the guys from Jersey or New York and California and like that, they would ship them to Mississippi and Georgia; you know, it was like they were trying to prove something. You know. So that's about all I know about the story about Lester.
I've read
After Lester got out of ... in-Red
People's account says he was never quite the same; it was like a permanent scar; the experience in the army. Is that the way you found him, too?

No, I don't really think that's true. No. I don't really think that's true. He wasn't a person that I found was really vindictive; he didn't carry hate around with him, and if he did -- if he did, his music wouldn't be the way it came out. I don't think that you can play so beautifully and then have all of that.
Well, I don't mean that I read anything that said he was full of hate, but, rather, that he had a broken spirit from having been mistreated.

Well, I think ... but I think that it lasted like a year or two, but I don't think a man can carry that type of thing for -- I don't think he was the type of person, I'm saying. Because I don't think it was of that magnitude, I don't -- I know it was rough on him, but it was rough on a lot of guys, you know. But I don't think it left on scars on Lester. I think that he was more intelligent than that.

Leonard Feather says that right before he went back to Paris, that you went to New York, and I believe the word he used was that you had 'upbraided him' or not taking care of business, and told him to straighten up or something. Is that true?

Yeah, well, you know, you got to remember that he was my older brother, and as far as the word -- I think that's a bad word, 'upbraiding' him, because I would not do that with him, because I had an awful lot of respect for him.

Because it was our teaching, you know ... no, I couldn't do it. It was done, but it was not done in that manner. It's a bad choice of words. But it's just -- well, he was not a good businessman, you know; he was just a true artist. And they could take advantage of him from every angle that you could think of, you know.

I'll tell you something on this tape -- and then I'm gonna close out with this. But let me tell you something. I'm in the recording business, right? I think and I see where musicians that are deceased, I think it's just criminal what the record companies do and the people that have the masters, what they get away with, by putting these people's music out and with no accounting to the estate, no accounting to anything.

So there's a fellow who's getting ready to do a thing on Lester -- do all of Lester's solos as they did Charlie Parker's thing -- and all of the songs that Lester has written is in to this publishing company. I'm gonna take all of the songs and put them in my publishing company; the same songs with the same arrangements, and I'm gonna make them come after me. Because I'm gonna get them for

Lester Junior. But I'm gonna make them fight for it. So I'm gonna copyright the same things, you know? So I just wanted -- you don't have to keep this for posterity, but I mean that, because it's an unfair situation.

You see everybody has something out on him now, and his family gets nothing. Because they don't understand, and they do this in the record business all the time. They don't get an accounting for the music they've written, they don't get accounting for the performances -- so they can tell Mary or Lester, 'Oh, I paid him when he did this. There was no royalty deal.'

But there's no such thing as no royalty deal. Now that I'm in the record business, I know that when a person performs and if they are the artist, there is a royalty deal someplace. So if you don't have one now, you can make one. And that's really the way I feel about it, because I'm going to take the same songs, the same arrangements, and I'm going to copyright them and I'm gonna put them in my publishing company, which is called Flipside, when you see Flipside, you'll know -- that I will get the money and I will give it to Lester's son and his wife.
But I'll make them come after it. Because I know how to fight them about it. But see, they don't have a clue. You got to fight them about it.
When did you get in to the record
business? I was first aware of it with Vee Jay, but was that the first record company you were with?
No, when I left Nat in '62, and in March in Mexico City, I came home and I didn't know what I wanted to do. I knew I didn't want to play music any more.
MS. WILLARD: Why?

Well, I've always had a thing -- I always wanted to end up on top of anything I'd do; I want to remember being at the top. I don't want someone -- I didn't want anyone to remember me later on, saying, in '77, say, you really should have heard him play in '54 or '55. Because I had lived with that all of my life; I'd always told my wife and my son that I would not be sitting up on the bandstand like Zooty, Zooty, for instance -- you know, Zooty played until he was in the seventies.

That's admirable, but to me, it's kind of pitiful, too; I know that's the man's life, but I think that a man is put here to do more than one thing, you know, and I never thought of myself as being one dimensional, and I believe that I can learn to do anything, and when I came off the road, I went to -- Andy Williams called me because he had somebody in New York -- or Chicago -- that couldn't play his music, and he must have called me 7 or 8 times, because I didn't want to play any more.
And so he made me a proposition I could not refuse, and so I went and I stayed for 3 weeks, and I came back in '62 -- and that was the last time that I played.
Around July or August, I formed a record company
called Melic -- M-e-l-i-c. That was my record company.
That's right, called me once and
That was when you were looking for Ethel Waters. And we found her in Pasadena.
(Interruption)
That's right. And so I started Melic record label, and I had 2 publishing companies; one in BMI called Flipside and the other in ASCAP called Land Lee. Well, I recorded some people.

You know, speaking of Ethel Waters, I thought -- my thing about looking for Ethel Waters at the time, I thought it would be a good idea, because I'll tell you, my first time away from home, I went away from home with here, and I thought in my mind it would be a good thing to get here and record her. But after I -- I did find her in Pasadena, incidentally -- after I went out and talked to her, then I began to learn a little more about the record business, and I knew it would not be a good idea to record her, so instead of her, I found Damita Jo, and I did an album on Damita Jo.
She sang at the Oasis when your band was there, didn't she?

No. No. She was at the [Belle Tavern.] See, she was at the [Belle Tavern] when Ernie was there -- Marshall's brother -- Ernie Royal. That was her first job. She auditioned, when she was like, 18 years old -- from Santa Barbara. But no, she didn't do the Oasis with me. I made an album with her and Dave Grusin did the arrangements.

And that was in '63. I didn't know anything about the record business at all -- was scared to death. Twentieth Century Fox wanted to give me $20,000 advance for the album, and I wouldn't take it because I thought they were going to ...
(Interruption)
Damita Jo was ...

Yeah. So, you know, if you don't have knowledge of something, then you suspect -- and I'd heard so many stories how they take your records and -- one of the biggest mistakes I made in my life was not taking that money! Because I put the record out myself, and they really took me pretty good, because the pressing plants get you when you're new; I had to pay 13¢ a record, and after I found about it later when I was accepted, I didn't have to pay but 9¢, you know. And you ship these records to Cleveland; to all the different places all over.

I sent 10,000 to Cleveland. This is a funny story, I think; this was when I really got my feet wet! I shipped this fellow 10,000 in Cleveland, and I kept billing him and wondering when he's gonna send me my money. So he told me, I'm gonna ship you your records back because I didn't sell but 300 and something so he paid me for 300 and something, and the records were sitting up in my office, and I said, now what I should do is take these singles and use them as demos, you know, to get somebody else to record the song. The title of the song was "It Kills Me", she was singing.
Was it a new song?
Yeah. Howlett Smith was on my publishing company -- I don't know if you know him; he's a blind pianist; do you know him? Yeah, he wrote the song.

And so I said what I should do, I said, I should use these as demos. And so I broke the box open, and I reached down and I took about 15 or 20, but after the first 3, the next 17 were, you know, Gene Autry's records, anybody's records you could think of, and I started breaking the box open, and they'd put 3 of mine on top, and everything else was old time, you know, Freddie Slack records, anything. So that was really my baptism to what the record business was all about.
Wasn't there anything you could do about that?

No, there wasn't anything I could do. That's why they tell you -- independents eat you alive in the record business; if you are a small record company. That's why Motown records, you know, this is where I work now, not only an oddity but they were very fortunate because they came along at the right time. And they were in a place where they were one of a kind, you know, Motown was the only record company in Detroit. So they had that where they could make it. But for an independent record company to make it, the distributors would eat you alive.
See, what they will do is they won't pay you, but

they'll pay all the big companies. You know, they'll pay the big companies, so you don't have much of a shot, so I don't think -- and after I fooled with my company a little while, then the President, Randy Wood, called me at VeeJay and wanted me to come to work for VeeJay records.
Now I had never worked for a record company in my life, and so ...
MS. WILLARD: There're 2 Randy Woods--

Yeah, there's one black and one white. Well, this was the black one -- VeeJay, right. So after I was there about a year and 3 months, you know, remember VeeJay had all the first Beatle records; all the first Beatle records, because Randy made the deal, which was a heck of a deal he made.

But after a year and 3 months, they closed down and moved back to Chicago. And from there, I went to UA, which is Liberty Records, and I ran the budget line there, which was called Sunset. There was a Sunset label, and I run the budget line -- it was $1.99 album, and so I had to package it all together, which was really great experience.
And while I was working there ..,
Were these new recordings or were they reissues?
No, they were reissues. And it was great experience, because it gave me a chance to meet all the different publishers, because I used to talk to them about rates all over the country.

But a record came out, "Oh Happy Day" at the time, and so Jay [Flasko] over at Dunhill, he's a great marketing man, and so he saw the marketing people that were doing this record had slipped up on something, and so he called me on a Friday and told me he wanted an album on the street by Monday and could I do it.

He wanted 10 religious songs, but he wanted "Oh Happy Day" in it, and he said he had the cover ready, and could I get the record. And I had him hold on the phone and I got in touch -- incidentally, the young man works here now, James Carmichael, who produces the Commodores -- well, James Carmichael and another fellow named Arthur Wright who is now producing the Pips, well I called both of them -- they were both pretty heavy in to the church, and I told him what we wanted to do, and did they think we could pull it off. And they said yes.

So I used 10 musicians and about 35 singers, and we went to Radio Recorders, and one would rehearse the singers and the other would rehearse the band. And I had 3 copies over in the corner; they were copying the music as we did it. And now what he had detected, that they had Edwin Hawkins -- it said the Edwin Hawkins Singers on their album; you know, the people who did "Oh Happy Day" -- so all he had on his was "Oh Happy Day".
So anyway, to make a long story short, we got it

out; I had it on his desk Monday morning, and he got the album and they put it all over Wallach's Music City, in the window, and see, people were buying "Oh Happy Day". They would go in and say, "Give me Oh Happy Day". So they didn't know who the guy was, you know, and on the one that I did, I had a woman singing it, and that's how I left UA to go to Dunhill Records. Because I told him that -- I said, "Well, doing this for you and working for another record company, I may lose my gig." He said, "If you lose your gig, come to me."
And so I prevaricated and told them they were giving me a lot of heat, and so I went over -- because I wanted to change jobs. And that's how I went over to ABC.
You joined ABC when?

In '69. And I stayed until '73, and in June, I came to Motown, and in '73, and I stayed at Motown I was always the head of A & R. 7 weeks, and went back to ABC. And then last January 15, 1977, I came back to Motown. Now don't be surprised in 1978 I go back to ABC.
At what point in your record company career did your son join you in the legal department? I know he's an attorney, right?
Yeah. Well, what happened -- my son was at the City Attorney's office, and I told him that I thought that he probably should go into entertainment law, you know.

I got him, probably pointed in that direction - we both attended USC and took a course in entertainment law one year, and it was kind of interesting to him, so that was just a way to give him a little feel of the thing.

And I heard that they needed an attorney out at Universal MCA, and I'd known a guy over there for years, and I called him and asked him, what about Lee, and he had known Lee since he was 6 or 7 years old -- and he was so surprised that he had turned out to be an attorney, so he said, 'Well, send him out.'

So I sent him out and he went out and they hired him. Well, he stayed there 2½ years, and then I was on a plane going to New York when I did the Broadway play, Two Gentlemen of Verona, and I recorded that in New York. And so I was commuting back and forth, and so I met the head counsel of ABC on the plane; we went back there together and he was from New York and he was saying that he was looking for an attorney to take over the west coast of ABC, and so I told him I just happened to have one for him.

And then he interviewed Lee and he hired Lee, and made Lee chief counsel and head of the legal department, and he had 4 other attorneys working under him. That was I think '71 ... no ... yeah, '71 it was when he came over.
So then he worked there until he came to Motown, and he came to Motown in October of '76, and don't be surprised
if he leaves, too! (Interruption) I was about to ask you what artists do you work with at Motown?
Oh, at Motown here, I don't work with any artists.
But when I called to make this appointment to do this, they told me I wanted the publishing department.

Well, no. What I am here, I am the -- I'm in charge of all the budgets here, okay? All the recording budgets. So what happens if someone -- they get ready to go in the studio, they want to record, so they come in and they sit with me, and we go over the budget. Now if they want $85,000 in the budget, then my job is to show them if it shouldn't be but $65,000 ---so being a musician and having had the experience in the studio, then I can generally show it to them, and -- but not always. Sometimes maybe we will take $85,000, you know -- it's according to who it is and where they're gonna do it.

But really my function here is -- it's more of an administrative thing. Creatively, you get involved with it because you're dealing with creative people, and the thing that I have going for me is when you sit and talk to a musician and tell him -- you got to know what you're talking about if he says he wants to use 24 strings, and you tell
him that you don't think he shoud use but 14, you know. Now you just can't sit there and say, well, what are you gonna use 24 for? You can use 18 and do the same thing.

So then you have to talk to him in musical terms and say, well, if you use double stops, you can use 12, and if you get the right musicians. So I can talk to them from that standpoint, musically, and I really don't have any problems with them. We've cut the budget considerably since I've been here.

Now over at ABC, the type of things that I always did -- I did all the soundtrack albums. I did Liza Minelli's "Cabaret" over there; I did "The Song of Norway", "Lovers and Other Strangers" -- and as I said before I went to New York, and I did the Broadway show, which we were up for a Grammy for it -- I think we came in 2nd, and nobody ever remembers 2nd -- but I'll tell you.

But I really came over here to do a jazz label. That was why I left ABC, because my deal here was we're gonna start a jazz label and I was going to do it. That's what I am supposed to start in January.
You are?
Yes, uh huh. That's what I was saying -- if you hear about me going to someplace else because they didn't start the jazz label..
Will it be called Motown? Do they have a name?
Well, we're trying to decide what it
will be called. We haven't come up with a name for it yet. But yeah, we're supposed to have it. As a matter of fact, there's a ...
That's exciting.
Well, there's a market for it.

Yeah, well, it's all over the street. I've had many, many calls from jazz musicians who want to come with us. But we'll see about that. You know, I did all the gospel over at ABC, also; I did that because I ran in to a lot of young people that I thought had a lot of talent, and no one was recording them, and so I just started recording them for Duke Peacock -- that's the label that ABC acquired.

But all in all, the only reason I changed jobs was because of the carrying of the jazz label. And if you get a chance to build it yourself, then I wont' have to sit around and say what's wrong with the things that Norman Granz Graham does, you know?
That would really be exciting.

I think it was kind of interesting, you were talking about back during the record band and Capitol was right over there, and I wasn't sitting close enough to the window to see, here on the 17th floor, of the United California Bank Building -- I wasn't sitting close enough to the window to be able to realize when you gestured that way, you are in a position here so that you can look down right on top of the building that was Capitol Records.
That's right.

I mean you can look down on RCA from where I'm sitting, but over there you can see the front door of what used to be Capitol Records, and the back door. And here in your office, which is decorated by giant photo murals of golf courses.
Of Pebble Beach and Monterey Peninsula. That's the 18th hole at Pebble Beach, and that's the 16th hole at Monterey Peninsula.
Where did you get them?
I bought them from a guy up north. His name slips by, but I think they are great pictures, you know?
Oh, they're beautiful. You're a That's a golfball ashtray golf man, right?
Yeah, golf is my thing. I enjoy that. Anything more?
Not unless you want to talk about your specific plans for ... the jazz label.
I don't think so. I'll wait to see if it happens. If it happens, then I will have plenty to say about it.
You mentioned earlier that you had recorded someone in Mexico City and there was something significant about facilities there.
Oh yes. I did. Well, when I was with ABC, there was a young lady who came in, and she had $30,000

and she wanted somebody -- someone sent her to me and told her I better give her some direction because she's running around with this $30,000 check -- and I have a reputation in the business as honest John, you know, so I'll try to direct somebody in the right direction.

So she wanted to sing, and she was a singer, as a matter of fact -- but she wanted to record here in L.A., and I gave her some names, of people, and she kept coming back and she says, "But why can't you do it?" And I kept saying to her, "Well, I don't really want to do it." And she said that she was gonna go to Mexico, and it was almost time for me to have a vacation, you know, so she said she was going to Mexico to work at this club.

So I said, "If you go to Mexico to work at that club, this is where you should record." I remember the man that got us the musicians when I was with Nat down there -- he was supposed to be the greatest musician in Mexico; everybody looks up to him in Mexico City.
Who was that?
Remember his name?

I'm trying to think .. I'll get his name for you, but so she said, 'Well, would you come to Mexico and record me there?' I said, "Well, let me tell you now, we can make a deal -- because I'm going on vacation, and I was going to Mexico on vacation; Mexico City" -- but the $30,000 it would cost her here, I told her it wouldn't cost more than

$15,000 there -- which it would not. So she says, 'Well, what are you gonna charge me?' And I said, 'The only thing I will charge you for is you pick up my hotel tab and you pick up my golf tab.' That was all, you know. So anybody would say yes to that, but I don't know if she knew that it cost me $50 a day to play golf in Mexico City and I was there 3 weeks and I played every day. But you know, if it costs you $50 a day -- well, and I had a nice pad, but I recorded her there.

But my experience with the musicians there were unreal. Unreal. Ernie Freeman made all the charts for me, and I took the charts down there, and Ernie writes not easy for guitars, you know, and he wrote these guitar parts, and I took them down there and I recorded everything at once; I didn't lay tracks. You know, I didn't do rhythm sections and then the horns and strings -- I did everything at once, and the thing really turned out good. And the musicians were a pleasant surprise. They were unreal.

They walked in and they cut that music, and they were playing these rock things he had written just like you were in America playing it. So, you know, the world has become very, very small from shipping records, one country knows what another country is doing.
How about the recording facilities?
RCA. Very good. Just what we have here, they have it there. And if you want to go and see, where
I think the best recording facilities are, you got to go to Germany.
Where about?
Munich, Hamburg -- they really -- I think they're kind of a little ahead of us, you know, in those types of things. I think they are.
Have you recorded there, or ...

Now, what happened was I was doing -- there was a time in between jobs where I was doing -- I used to do for about a year for Germany and Japan the top 12 hits of Billboard. I had a deal with the guy who used to ship them to Japan, and Germany -- but it would be the top 12 of Billboard.

Now what you had to do -- I would do this every week, the top 12, but I got better at that than I am at the racing form, you know? Because you got to guess what's gonna end up being up there. See, if you record the 12 this week, now you know some of those songs remain the next week. Now I've got to get 12 for the next week, and I have to have them every week. So you had to really live with the charts, and try to decide what's gonna be there 3 weeks from now. You know? And you'd be surprised what kind of record -- I had doing that thing.
I got so good at it -- really -- there was one song that came on the charts, what's the guy's name, it was about his wife, one of the best songs -- it jumped; it came on, like,

50, and then it went to like, 10 -- and do you know, I recorded it the second week. "Honey" -- that was it. It was a smash. "Honey" -- just a great song, and it just took the 2nd week, I grabbed it, and it jumped up there, you know, and I heard every record -- heard more records then than I do now, you know; had to listen to everything. We did things -- Aretha was hot then; and I kept a stable.

I had a male singer, a female singer, a female group, a male group and a 6 piece band -- and we would go in every Saturday, every Saturday -- and made quite a bit of money with it. Made quite a bit of money with it. Did it for about a year and 3 months.
Was that somehow related to the ....

Yes. Better finish the story. Why it's related to the German studio, when we used to send these tapes to Germany and send them to Japan, the German people started sending us things back, and telling us what was wrong with our sound, and would play things and send them back on the tape and tell us, this is what it should sound like, and it was no comparison. The fidelity, you would not believe. You would not believe it. I mean, just unreal. Unreal. They would copy, I'm saying, the stuff that I had sent them -- and when they got through turning their knobs, whatever their knobs had on them, they never asked us to play what we sent them and play what they sent us back also. Then you just wouldn't believe it.

segments.title: Copyright notice, Smithsonian oral history title page and Reel 1 heading.
segments.summary: Copyright warnings and the Smithsonian title page for Lee Young's interview with Patricia Willard, Reel 1, November 8, 1977.

segments.title: Lee Young's name Leonidas and how his father chose it
segments.summary: Willard asks about his full name; he explains it was given by his schoolteacher father, who liked Greek history, and that he went by Lee from high school.

segments.title: Born in New Orleans; father William Handy Young the multi-instrumentalist
segments.summary: Born March 7, 1917, in New Orleans; his father was a bandleader and teacher who played piano, brass, strings, and especially saxophone (C Melody).

segments.title: Father's pupils Clarence Williams and Cootie Williams; the Lackman and Carson carnival
segments.summary: His father taught Clarence Williams and Cootie Williams; the family traveled on a carnival with Lester and Irma playing in the band.

segments.title: Ben Webster learns saxophone from Lester and the elder Young
segments.summary: In Albuquerque Ben Webster came as a poor pianist, so Lee's father taught him saxophone, practicing alongside Lester.

segments.title: Early show business: father takes the children on the road
segments.summary: Lee says he was in show business as long as he can remember, left New Orleans at about five after his parents separated, and sang and danced as a child.

segments.title: Seeing Bill Bojangles Robinson dance in wooden shoes
segments.summary: He recalls seeing Bojangles Robinson at a medicine show and Willard asks how the wooden-soled dancing shoes worked.

segments.title: The TOBA circuit and its stars
segments.summary: The family worked the TOBA circuit through the South and Midwest, sharing bills with Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith and others, where Lee really learned to dance.

segments.title: Dance contests judged by sound alone
segments.summary: He describes dance contests where judges sat below the stage and judged only the sound of the feet, and compares it to judging artists on tape.

segments.title: Minneapolis, his father's big band, and Lester practicing Trumbauer records
segments.summary: The family settled in Minneapolis where his father formed a 13-piece band; Lee sang and Lester practiced constantly to Frankie Trumbauer records.

segments.title: The family saxophone band and Lester cutting Cousin Boots
segments.summary: Corrects the saxophone trio story: the band was his parents and two cousins; young Lester crashed a dance and outplayed Cousin Boots.

segments.title: Not wanting to play: his father supplies instruments
segments.summary: Lee wanted sports, but in the house everybody played, and his father kept producing instruments until he learned.

segments.title: The yardstick trick: Lester faking reading music
segments.summary: Lester had great ears but would not read, so his father set a trap with the blackboard and hit him with a yardstick when caught.

segments.title: Cousins Sport and Boots and their influence on Lester
segments.summary: Willard checks the cousins' names with Jimmy Talbert's information; Lee sees them as adversaries to the young Lester, who challenged them at 12 or 13.

segments.title: Lester began on drums and held his sticks unusually
segments.summary: Lee started on drums again in Phoenix; he explains Lester played drums first and held a stick between forefinger and middle finger.

segments.title: Instruments in the family and niece Martha Young
segments.summary: Lester's first instrument was drums, Lee's saxophone; his mother played baritone; only niece Martha Young became a pianist.

segments.title: His stepmother Sarah and his natural mother Lizetta
segments.summary: His mother in the band was Sarah, his stepmother; his natural mother Lizetta Gray he did not see again until about 1941-42.

segments.title: Carnival life as a child: the Midway and Hey Rube
segments.summary: He describes carnival midways, side shows, the Hey Rube fight cry, hustling for dimes, and seeing nearly every state by age 13.

segments.title: How minstrel shows worked; Sophie Tucker selling her book
segments.summary: Tent minstrel shows ran full performances with 10-12 acts and sold photographs; he compares it to Sophie Tucker selling books in Miami in 1956.

segments.title: The Young kid act that nobody wanted to follow
segments.summary: The father's act featured Irma, Lester and Lee singing and dancing; Lee as a comic made the music stop for thrown coins.

segments.title: The all-black minstrel show on a white carnival and the Sword Lady box
segments.summary: Their minstrel show was the only black attraction on the carnival; his sister was put in the sword box illusion.

segments.title: Phoenix and Lester running away from home
segments.summary: In Phoenix the family played West Lake Park; Lester, who could not be beaten into line, ran away repeatedly, once returning as they bought train tickets.

segments.title: Their father's acceptance of Lester's individuality
segments.summary: Lee reflects that their father recognized Lester was different and that the parents encouraged individuality in all three children.

segments.title: Lee as a child blackface comic
segments.summary: He describes his blackface costume and makeup as a small boy in minstrel shows and carnivals.

segments.title: Minstrel show structure, TOBA blackface comics and Al Jolson
segments.summary: He explains the interlocutor and end-men layout, says black comics on TOBA wore blackface, and mentions later recording music for The Jolson Story.

segments.title: More on Bill Robinson and Lee's poor memory for years
segments.summary: He says he cannot date events, only incidents, and recalls Robinson running backwards faster than others ran forward.

segments.title: Dancing and drumming, and getting an MGM job through dancing
segments.summary: Drummers such as Buddy Rich, Louie Bellson and Jo Jones danced; Lee says dancing got him an MGM job on Strike Up the Band.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Singing at Curtis Mosby's Apex Club at age 13
segments.summary: Arriving in Los Angeles, Lee won a guest night at the Apex Club, where Ivie Anderson and Eddie Anderson worked, and was hired by Curtis Mosby.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Child labor law ends his club job; the dancer Jack Williams
segments.summary: The Labor Commission stopped Lee and the dancer Jack Williams working at the club, after which Lee turned seriously to music.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Landing the job with Papa Mutt Carey on Louisiana ties
segments.summary: Living next to the Musicians Union on Central Avenue, Lee got the drummer job with Papa Mutt Carey without playing, simply because his father was Professor Young from New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Filling in for married drummers at five black bands
segments.summary: Lee worked free on nights off for drummers in five bands at Long Beach and elsewhere to gain experience before the Papa Mutt job.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Reel 2 heading and continuation
segments.summary: Smithsonian heading for Reel 2, dated November 8-9, 1977, and a pickup from the previous day.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: C.P. Johnson's band at the Wave Cafe on the Long Beach pier
segments.summary: He played at the Wave Cafe with C.P. Johnson, Jack McVea and Alton Redd, earning a share of a sailors' kitty larger than the salary.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Battle of the bands at the Apex: Buck Clayton versus Les Hite
segments.summary: He recalls Buck Clayton's Fourteen Gentlemen of Harlem facing Les Hite's Cotton Club band, listing Hite's sidemen, and Clayton's band being stranded in China.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: First big band: Buck Clayton's Fourteen Gentlemen at the Club Arabee
segments.summary: Lee joined Buck Clayton's band at the Club Arabee as its youngest and got a harsh reading lesson from guitarist Frank Pasley.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Hershel Evans in the band and dating Buck Clayton's group
segments.summary: Lee and Willard work out from Chilton that Buck Clayton and Hershel Evans left for Basie in 1936, so the Arabee band was about 1935.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Charlie Echols, the West Coast Cab Calloway
segments.summary: He describes Charlie Echols, a bandleader who could not play but fronted good musicians like Cab Calloway.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Touring with Ethel Waters and Eddie Mallory; marrying Louise Rankin
segments.summary: Lee auditioned to keep up with Lindy Hoppers, left home with Tyree Glenn and Don Byas, then quit after three weeks to marry Louise Rankin in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
segments.title: Los Angeles clubs and musician haunts in the thirties
segments.summary: He describes the drugstore at 43rd and Central, the Bell Tavern and Topsy's, and how many clubs hired piano-and-singer duos.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: The Famous Door, Stuff Smith and Sunday jam sessions
segments.summary: At the Famous Door near the Union he heard Stuff Smith's band in 1937 and joined the Sunday jam sessions.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Practicing rudiments every morning with Cozy Cole
segments.summary: He says he learned from every drummer, especially Cozy Cole, a rudimental practice enthusiast who drilled him from the book daily.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Fats Waller trio at the Famous Door; Fats as godfather
segments.summary: After Stuff Smith, Lee worked in a Fats Waller trio with bassist Al Morgan, and Fats became godfather to his son.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Eddie Barefield's rehearsal band
segments.summary: Eddie Barefield stayed in Los Angeles and formed a band with Paul Howard, Jack McVea and Dudley Brooks that rehearsed with new arrangements daily.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Don Byas writes a slow Dinah at the Cotton Club
segments.summary: He recalls Don Byas in Barefield's band at the Cotton Club, where Byas arranged Dinah slowly in a minor key.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Recording with the Nat Cole trio for Decca
segments.summary: After Barefield, Lee joined Nat Cole's new trio for Decca dates, where he sang and played on The Black Spider.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Spike Jones and the measured music session
segments.summary: At a measured-music date, Spike Jones wanted Lee to play brushes on a drum case, which Lee refused.

segments.chapter: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
segments.title: Leaving Nat Cole for Les Hite: the Cubanola and Omar's Dome
segments.summary: Lee was Nat's first drummer, but after a short stint at the Swanee Inn he joined Les Hite's reduced band at the Cubanola and then Omar's Dome, singing ballads.

segments.title: First studio job: coaching Billy Lee for The Coconut Grove
segments.summary: His first studio job was recording the drums and teaching the child actor Billy Lee to mime them at Paramount.

segments.title: Winning the Strike Up the Band job by teaching Mickey Rooney
segments.summary: Lee beat other drummers for the MGM job by showing Mickey Rooney how to play the time step and break on drums.

segments.title: Playing the soundstage solo from memory while sitting on the music
segments.summary: Lee recorded the featured drum part with a 45-piece orchestra and, to be noticed, sat on his music and played it from memory.

segments.title: Promised $500 but paid $66 for the drum recording
segments.summary: MGM had promised Lee $500 for the drum recording but paid union scale of $66 for two sessions, and he refused to work further.

segments.title: Hiding at Val Verde from the MGM music head
segments.summary: Lee and Jimmy Blanton hid in Val Verde while MGM sent a limousine to find him because only he could teach Mickey the solos.

segments.title: Negotiating $25 an hour in Louis B. Mayer's office
segments.summary: In a meeting in Mayer's office Lee got his $500 and demanded $25 an hour, not scale, for teaching Mickey Rooney.

segments.title: Mickey Rooney on drums, Jackie Cooper and MGM's big office
segments.summary: Willard and Lee discuss Rooney learning drums, Jackie Cooper being the actor who could play, and who agreed to Lee's terms.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: A trip to New York with his drums, jamming and sitting in with Basie
segments.summary: Lee took his drums on a bus to New York, met Freddie Green, Jo Jones, J.C. Heard and others, and sat in with Basie in Brooklyn.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: The Paradise Club and the Clarence Profit Trio
segments.summary: He tells of the Paradise on Main Street, where Goodman found Hampton, and says he told Nat Cole not to join Hampton's band after hearing the Clarence Profit Trio.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Joining Lionel Hampton's new band as drummer and singer
segments.summary: Hampton formed his band with Sir Charles, Vernon Alley and Irving Ashby; Lee sang, beat Billy Eckstine in the Pittsburgh Courier poll, and left in early 1941.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Hampton as leader: jealousy and the Diggy Diggy Doo challenge
segments.summary: Lee admits jealousy of Hamp, a drummer himself, and describes their closing number of trading fours.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Forming his own band at Billy Berg's as Lester arrives
segments.summary: After Hamp, Lee formed a band with Red Callender and Bumps Myers at Billy Berg's, and the union moved to restrict Lester's playing when he came out.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Reel 3 heading
segments.summary: Smithsonian heading for Reel 3, dated November 9-10, 1977.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Union forces Lester to play from the floor as a guest
segments.summary: Because of the separate locals, Lester had to wait on a milk box and play three tunes in each set from the floor for six weeks while his transfer went through.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: The four-part sound: Gerald Wilson, Dudley Brooks and Strayhorn arrange
segments.summary: The band of trumpet, two tenors and guitar attracted arrangers Gerald Wilson, Dudley Brooks and Billy Strayhorn, and got a Cafe Society offer, but never recorded.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Sunday jam sessions at Billy Berg's and the $500 union fine
segments.summary: Lee ran jam sessions, was fined $500 after one that brought in players from the Ellington and Lunceford bands, and lived next to the Union.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Billy Berg's moves to the Trouville; Billie Holiday works with the band
segments.summary: Billy Berg's next club, the Trouville on Beverly across from CBS, had Billie Holiday and Jimmy Rowles with Lee's band on a late schedule.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Sunday jam sessions at the Trouville
segments.summary: Each Sunday the Nat Cole trio and Lee backed tenor, alto and trumpet players in sessions that Lee says Los Angeles started.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Norman Granz, tennis and the origin of Jazz at the Philharmonic
segments.summary: Lee gave Granz names of musicians to call; Granz took the idea to clubs and Lee believes this led to Jazz at the Philharmonic.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Jamming at the Union against the separate locals' rules
segments.summary: Lee describes being brought before the board for jamming and holding daily noon jam sessions in the practice hall, dodging the walking delegate Elmer Fayne.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Art Tatum and the after-hours piano sessions
segments.summary: He describes after-hours houses where local pianists played in turn before Tatum, who loved whist and beer.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Oscar Peterson meets Art Tatum at Gerald Wiggins's house
segments.summary: Lee tells how Oscar Peterson played for 35-40 minutes before Tatum took over and ended with Little Man You've Had a Busy Day.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Going to track meets with Art Tatum
segments.summary: Lee never played with Tatum but walked with him at track meets, where he reacted to a pole vault before the crowd did.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: The successive Billy Berg's clubs and the scale of Los Angeles music
segments.summary: Lee lists Billy Berg's moves from Pico and La Cienega to Beverly, Hollywood Boulevard and Vine, stressing how much music LA had.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Leaving Cafe Society when his father fell ill
segments.summary: After two or three months at Cafe Society, Lee left the band to go home because his father was gravely ill.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Skipping his own opening night to play with Duke Ellington
segments.summary: On opening night at Billy Berg's, Lee left his own band to sub for Sonny Greer with Ellington at the Trianon, to Billy Berg's astonishment.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: How Duke starts the band, and the $17.50 pay
segments.summary: Lee explains Ellington cued the band through his runs on the piano, and says he was paid about $17.50 for the night.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: First seeing Lester as an adult at their father's illness
segments.summary: Lester came from Kansas City in Basie's car and chauffeur; Lee woke to find his high-voiced brother.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Lester's dog Tonics
segments.summary: Lester stayed about ten days with a black Belgian police dog named Tonics, which Lee eventually left far out where Watts is now.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: His father's death and the end of the band
segments.summary: Lee's father died around 1942 or 1943, and the band was not kept together after he came home from New York.

segments.chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
segments.title: Judy Holliday's act at Cafe Society
segments.summary: He recalls Clyde Hart sitting in and a comedy act of Judy Holliday that shared the Cafe Society bill.

segments.title: Tape break and return to Lester
segments.summary: After a tape cut on November 10, Willard asks Lee to talk about how Lester evolved from the Minneapolis days.

segments.title: Lester's reputation when he joined Lee's band
segments.summary: Lee first heard Basie records without knowing it was Lester; by the time he joined the small group, Lester was well known from his records.

segments.title: Lee on Norman Granz's recordings of Lester
segments.summary: Lee thinks Lester's later records under Granz, mostly blues, were almost demeaning and failed to show his scope as a ballad player.

segments.title: Lester's melodic ballad playing and Come Rain or Come Shine
segments.summary: Lee asked for Come Rain or Come Shine on a Granz session and praises Lester's melodic ballad playing that lay people could follow.

segments.title: Lester as a stylist who played to please himself
segments.summary: Lee says Lester's music was personal; he would not imitate Coleman Hawkins at Fletcher Henderson's, and Lee preferred to hear him in hard keys and ballads.

segments.title: How Lester's playing and personality changed
segments.summary: Lee describes Lester as a fast scale-running player on alto who changed on tenor, and as a soft-spoken introvert from childhood.

segments.title: Ralph Gleason's writing and Lester's private language and nicknames
segments.summary: Lee thinks only Ralph Gleason captured Lester and discusses Lester's slang and nicknames like Ripty Gipty for Paul Campbell.

segments.title: Lester's way at jam sessions, and the Bumps Myers legend
segments.summary: Lester did not want chords called to him and was proclaimed President; the idea that Bumps Myers could cut him proved absurd.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: CBS radio show with Rafael Mendez and a tuba Flight of the Bumblebee
segments.summary: Lee recalls a CBS show with Rafael Mendez, where a tuba player played the opening of Flight of the Bumblebee.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Freelancing in the studios as the only black musician; Calvin Jackson
segments.summary: At MGM and Columbia Lee played for dancers like Astaire, was the only black musician in the studios, and recalls Calvin Jackson denied composer credit.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Ray Heindorf, Lunceford at Warners and bringing in black players
segments.summary: Lee freelanced all over town, praises Ray Heindorf's support for black bands, and brought Marshall Royal and others to the studios.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Hired for the Camel Caravan then replaced the next week
segments.summary: After rehearsing and playing a CBS Camel Caravan show to congratulations, Lee returned the next Friday to find another drummer's set up.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: The DownBeat headline and the transfer rule violated for Nick Fatool
segments.summary: DownBeat headlined Color loses Lee Young's job; Lee believes it happened because of separate locals, since Nick Fatool took his job within days of arriving.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: The Union board hearing over the Camel job
segments.summary: The black press picked up the story and Lee argued before the union board that he understood his dates, despite his local's president suggesting he was mistaken.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Freddie Fisher testifies for Lee; the cost and pioneering
segments.summary: Conductor Freddie Fisher appeared unasked to confirm hiring Lee; Lee was paid for 13 shows but felt the principle was unresolved.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Black musicians absent from radio except guest stars
segments.summary: Lee says he was the only black radio musician, apart from guests like Louis Armstrong with Bing Crosby.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Reel 4 heading
segments.summary: Smithsonian heading for Reel 4, dated November 10, 1977.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Duke and Blanton on radio, and when Lee went on staff
segments.summary: Lee recalls Duke and Blanton on Bing Crosby's show and says he joined Columbia's staff in 1945 or 1946.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Running and padlocking a San Francisco club
segments.summary: In San Francisco Lee took over a club whose owner owed taxes, paid weekly toward them for ten weeks, then padlocked it after a dispute with a partner.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Who was in the San Francisco band
segments.summary: Lee names his band's tenor player Woodman and trumpeter Bates and a woman pianist he picked up in San Francisco.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: The Downbeat Club on Central Avenue and Mingus on bass
segments.summary: Back in Los Angeles Lee led bands at the Downbeat Club, with Charles Mingus on bass, down the street from Johnny Otis.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Stan Kenton's offer versus the Columbia staff job
segments.summary: Lee agreed to join Stan Kenton but contractor Dave Klein urged him to take the Columbia staff job, which he did to stay with his son.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Columbia Studios music department: Stoller and Bakaleinikoff
segments.summary: Lee describes Morris Stoll and Misha Bakaleinikoff at Columbia, and the practice of reusing music, which was banned in 1977.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: First day on staff at Columbia: five timpani for an Ann Miller picture
segments.summary: His first Columbia picture required him to play melodic timpani parts, so he arrived early to study the music.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Studying timpani and teaching himself xylophone
segments.summary: Lee studied timpani with Mr. White and taught himself xylophone because studio drummers had to be more than traps players.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Setting up the timpani; The Jolson Story and Rita Hayworth films
segments.summary: Lee worked out how to arrange five timpani for crossovers and played traps on musicals including The Jolson Story.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Concerts with Benny Goodman's small group
segments.summary: Benny Goodman asked for Lee, and with Mel Powell, Red Callender and Red Norvo he played concerts at the Shrine and Long Beach.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Confronting Benny Goodman about where the drums sit
segments.summary: Lee refused to sit far from the quintet at the Shrine, knocked on Goodman's dressing-room door, and got the drums placed where he wanted.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: Turning down Bob Crosby's radio show on Dave Klein's advice
segments.summary: Offered three times the money on Bob Crosby's CBS show, Lee stayed on staff because Dave Klein said leaving would hurt the next black musician.

segments.chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
segments.title: No other black musician on staff; Lionel Newman and Benny Carter
segments.summary: Lee says no other black musician joined the Columbia staff, and Benny Carter declined a Fox composer-arranger offer from Lionel Newman.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: The seven-piece band at the Casbah
segments.summary: At the Casbah Lee led a seven-piece band with Maxwell Davis, Marshall Royal and others that played big-band arrangements and Dizzy's Manteca.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: Dating the Casbah and Oasis years; the two record bands
segments.summary: Lee and Willard work out dates for Sarah Vaughan's Black Coffee, Lee's move to Nat in 1953, and the late-1940s record band.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: The record band and Kay Starr's hits recorded at Capitol
segments.summary: Lee describes recording in the Capitol president's office, where two Kay Starr hits were made, and earning two or three hundred dollars a session.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: Hal Stanley's clubs: Rum Boogie, Downbeat and the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Lee and Willard list the clubs Kay Starr's husband Hal Stanley ran, including a Hollywood Cotton Club that opened with Basie in February 1949.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: Kay Starr's $6,500 ring and the club's closing
segments.summary: Hal Stanley wanted Kay Starr's ring to keep the club open another week; she refused and the club closed.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: Leading the house band at The Oasis; Billy Eckstine and Mingus
segments.summary: Lee led the Oasis house band for about two years, backing Louis, Nat, Billie Holiday and Eckstine, whose song Mingus interrupted with his bow.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: The intimate Oasis combo with Par Jones, Ernie Freeman, Maxwell Davis
segments.summary: At the Oasis Lee used trumpet with a hat or mute, tenor, piano, brushes and bass so patrons could talk and dance.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: What became of the measured-music recordings; Nat's early singing
segments.summary: Lee does not know where the measured-music tracks went and says the group sang in unison; Nat later coached girl singers.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: His Club Alabam band with Art Pepper and Nat Cole's arrangements
segments.summary: At the Club Alabam Lee led a nine-piece integrated band with Art Pepper and Jack McVea, and Nat wrote pencil arrangements for $8 or $10 each.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: Playing the Alabam five times and demanding pay before going on
segments.summary: Curtis Mosby's Alabam had changing owners; Lee would not go on the bandstand until the box office paid him each night.

segments.chapter: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
segments.title: Lester hears Jimmy Blanton play Stardust
segments.summary: At the big session Lester, who only praised Slam Stewart, heard Blanton play bowed Stardust and exclaimed over the young bass player.

segments.title: Anchoring dates and Willard meeting Lee in 1949
segments.summary: Willard asks Lee to tie events to dates and notes they met in 1949 at Eddie Beal's house.

segments.title: Joining Nat Cole in June 1953
segments.summary: Lee accepted Nat's offer after several calls, opening at the Blue Note in Chicago and La Vie en Rose, then recording Twisted Stockings and Mona Lisa.

segments.title: Rehearsing the band at Ciro's and starting to conduct from the drums
segments.summary: Lee rehearsed Nat's band when Nat was away, and Nat began having Lee conduct from the drums.

segments.title: The 1954 London Palladium exchange with Ted Heath
segments.summary: The Palladium initially refused Lee's trio members, leading to a reciprocal exchange in which Ted Heath's band toured the States.

segments.title: The Ted Heath package tour and warnings about Birmingham
segments.summary: The package with Ted Heath, June Christie and Gary Morton was warned that Birmingham did not want white and black acts on one stage.

segments.title: The attack on Nat Cole on stage in Birmingham
segments.summary: Men rushed the stage and one hit Nat before detectives pulled him off; the next morning over 100 white people apologized at the airport.

segments.title: Stadium tour with Perry Como
segments.summary: A Pullman-car show with Nat and Perry Como played five stadiums before 35,000-40,000 people.

segments.title: South America 1960: Caracas, Rio and Buenos Aires musicians
segments.summary: Touring South America with a 20-piece book, Lee found the Buenos Aires players excellent, Rio's strings great and horns terrible.

segments.title: Mexico City, Uruguay and Rio
segments.summary: Lee compares Mexico City and Uruguay musicians and says recordings are leveling quality everywhere.

segments.title: Nat Cole gradually giving up piano
segments.summary: When Lee joined, Nat sat and played piano and sang in small clubs, then stood once they played bigger rooms like the Copacabana and Chez Paree.

segments.title: Reel 5 heading and Willard's follow-up questions
segments.summary: Reel 5 of November 15, 1977 opens with Willard saying she listened to the first four reels and wants to ask more about Lee's father.

segments.title: Father's Tuskegee education and black colleges in Louisiana
segments.summary: Lee says his father graduated from Tuskegee and relates how Grambling was founded with Booker T. Washington's help.

segments.title: Father as a school principal raising money from gamblers
segments.summary: His father was principal at a Louisiana school and got money from madams, pimps and dice games, who gave him cuts.

segments.title: Lee's youth baseball team and why hustlers helped the kids
segments.summary: Lee compares his father's fundraising to getting uniforms for his Los Angeles baseball team, helped mostly by gamblers like Black Dot McGee.

segments.title: Father's name: Willis or William Handy Young
segments.summary: Lee and Willard sort out whether the father's name was William or Willis Handy Young and whether Handy relates to W.C. Handy.

segments.title: Red Allen's father played with Lee's father in New Orleans
segments.summary: Willard cites Whitney Balliett that Red Allen's father and Lee's father worked together in New Orleans, which Lee had not known.

segments.title: Clarence Williams as his father's prize pupil
segments.summary: Lee recalls his father speaking of Big Head Clarence Williams, who went to New York, and wonders about Clarence Williams the Third.

segments.title: Father's drumming and refusing to cut two men to play the Orpheum circuit
segments.summary: His father also played drums, and in Minneapolis he turned down the Orpheum circuit rather than cut two players from his 11-piece band.

segments.title: The Pettiford family band in Minneapolis
segments.summary: Lee says Lester hung out with the Pettifords, who had a family band, but the two bands did not play together.

segments.title: Paternal grandparents in Natalbany, Louisiana
segments.summary: Lee recalls his grandfather the blacksmith and grandmother the evangelist on a farm near Hammond, Louisiana.

segments.title: Half sister and nephew Jimmy Talbert
segments.summary: Lee explains that his father's travels left him a half sister, mother of Jimmy Talbert and his brother.

segments.title: Niece Martha Young, jazz pianist in San Francisco
segments.summary: Lee describes his niece Martha, Irma's daughter, as a strong jazz pianist who played with Vi Redd.

segments.title: Lackman and Carson carnival, Ida Cox and Blind Denslow
segments.summary: They confirm the carnival name, discuss Ida Cox on minstrel shows, and Lee recalls the blind dancer Denslow.

segments.title: Lee as the comic, Lester as straight man, Irma leaving music
segments.summary: Lee played the comedian while Lester was straight man, and Irma stopped playing and went into singing and dancing.

segments.title: Los Angeles theatres and the Follies' black pit band
segments.summary: Irma worked at the Burbank Theatre; Lee recalls a black orchestra in the pit of the all-white Follies, where a white dancer was fired for speaking to a musician.

segments.title: How old Lester was when he left home
segments.summary: Lee says Lester first ran off at 11 or 12 to avoid his father's razor strap Greasy Jim, and left for good around 18 from Salina, Kansas.

segments.title: Stand-in band work on film sets and Earl Dancer
segments.summary: Lee explains black bands seen in films were often paid stand-ins, and recalls Earl Dancer directing a cabaret scene with the Nicholas Brothers.

segments.title: The Brownskin Models show and how Red Callender came west
segments.summary: Lee corrects the Brownskin Review to the Brownskin Models, a dancing and singing show, which brought Red Callender to the coast.

segments.title: His father conducting a WPA band and giving lessons in Los Angeles
segments.summary: In Los Angeles his father, too old to break into jazz, led a WPA band at a playground and taught free lessons, buying instruments from Mike Gould.

segments.title: Mike Gould's four generations and Lee's children and grandson
segments.summary: Mike Gould told Lee at a track meet that he had known four generations; Lee names his son Lee Jr., daughter Roslyn and grandson Mark.

segments.title: What the WPA band was and why it existed
segments.summary: Lee says the WPA band played band music and was a program to keep musicians and artists off the streets.

segments.title: Fact-checking Chilton: Ben Webster, Charlie Echols and the Famous Door
segments.summary: Willard checks Chilton details against Lee, including Albuquerque, Ben Webster's months with the band, Don Byas with Charlie Echols in 1936, and the Famous Door.

segments.title: Early Los Angeles bandleaders: Irving Brothers, Rebb Spikes, Earl Dancer, Edith Turnham
segments.summary: Lee responds to Chilton's names of early thirties Los Angeles bands and adds Edith Turnham, whose son Floyd played lead alto.

segments.title: School music: Polytechnic and Mrs. Goodrich teaching him to conduct
segments.summary: Lee says junior high music teacher Mrs. Goodrich had him glee club, drama and conducting the band, which later made conducting for Nat easy.

segments.title: Conductors he worked under and Phil Moore's Astaire film
segments.summary: Before Nat, Lee worked under the Bakaleinikoffs, Stoloff, Heindorf and others, and played drums for Phil Moore's score for Fred Astaire's One for My Baby.

segments.title: Freelance film dates: Hazel Scott, Lena Horne and Minnelli
segments.summary: Lee cannot name many films, but remembers dates for I Dood It with Hazel Scott, Lena Horne pictures, and a Minnelli scene with trumpeter Jack Trainer.

segments.title: Drum parts and night shooting with Louis Armstrong on a Mae West picture
segments.summary: Lee wrote march-with-four-feel drum parts for a Mae West film shot at night, where Louis Armstrong told stories between takes.

segments.title: Rival drummer Oscar Bradley and Lee's model Baby Lewis
segments.summary: Lee describes Lorenzo Flournoy's band at the Alabam and drummer Oscar Bradley who copied Lionel Hampton while Lee modeled himself on Baby Lewis.

segments.title: Lorenzo Flournoy and Dootsie Williams of Dootone Records
segments.summary: Flournoy played piano, and trumpeter Dootsie Williams later ran Dootone Records, selling party records and others from the back of his car.

segments.title: Group vocals and The Black Spider on the Decca sides
segments.summary: Lee recalls the Decca sides with the Nat Cole trio's group vocals and the very fast Black Spider.

segments.title: The Local 767 band marching in the Labor Day parade
segments.summary: Marshall Royal's Local 767 band existed only for Los Angeles's Labor Day parade, in which Louis once played.

segments.title: Three flatbed trucks: Basie, Lunceford and the 767 band
segments.summary: In 1939 Basie's, Lunceford's and the 767 band rode trucks in the Labor Day parade and traded blasts, which Lee says showed Los Angeles was not behind musically.

segments.title: Guitarist Louis Gonzales and the Strayhorn arrangements
segments.summary: Lee explains his violinist-turned-guitarist school friend could read single-line parts, so Strayhorn, Wilson and Brooks wrote four-part arrangements, including a condensed Flamingo.

segments.title: Recovered names and corrections: Jim Conklin, Frank Comstock, Oasis personnel
segments.summary: Lee supplies the Capitol president Jim Conklin and arranger Frank Comstock and denies Eric Dolphy or Wilfred Middlebrooks played in his Oasis band.

segments.title: First dates with Nat Cole at the Tiffany Club
segments.summary: Lee says he played the Tiffany Club with Nat only briefly when he first joined, with no rehearsal, before the group left on the road.

segments.title: Subbing with the Oscar Peterson trio in Aspen and the snare drum prank
segments.summary: Shortly before Nat, Lee was whisked to Aspen to replace Irving Ashby with Peterson and Ray Brown, who hid his snare drum as a joke.

segments.title: Trombonist Baron Morehead and his Club Alabam band
segments.summary: Lee describes Baron Morehead as a short, older trombonist-bandleader who kept good musicians and a good book at the Alabam.

segments.title: Reel 6 heading
segments.summary: Smithsonian heading for Reel 6, dated November 15, 1977.

segments.title: Jimmy Blanton's greatness and the Dave Dexter review
segments.summary: Lee calls Blanton the top bass player of his time and recounts a bassist's letter rebuking Dave Dexter's DownBeat criticism.

segments.title: Jimmy Blanton's tuberculosis and death at Olive View
segments.summary: A checkup on a lark revealed Blanton's tuberculosis; Lee drove him to sanitariums until he died at Olive View.

segments.title: Nat Cole standing to sing with the piano as a prop
segments.summary: Willard asks who played piano after Nat stood up to sing; Lee says nobody did, Nat tinkered on stage and Buddy Cole played on records.

segments.title: The Japanese tour: hip audiences and copyist bands
segments.summary: On the Orient trip Nat's love songs brought the house down, and Japanese bands copied Miller, Goodman and Herman perfectly.

segments.title: Manila: the promoter's cars and the weak musicians
segments.summary: In Manila the promoter provided each member's make of car, and the local musicians were poor compared with Japan.

segments.title: Learning in Rio how well Lester was known after his death
segments.summary: Arriving in Rio in 1960 three months after Lester died, Lee was interviewed about his brother and was moved by his fame abroad.

segments.title: English discography of his dates; Nellie Lutcher and Goodman sextet sessions
segments.summary: English fans gave Lee a book of his record dates, reminding him of Nellie Lutcher, Dinah Shore and Benny Goodman sessions, and click-track studio work.

segments.title: Lester's army trouble and his white wife Mary
segments.summary: Lee says Lester's commanding officer was right that the wife in the locker photo was white, and that Lester could not adjust to orders.

segments.title: Lee's view of Lester's induction and the army's posting of black soldiers
segments.summary: Lee thinks Lester should have gone to a band like Great Lakes, recalls him jumping the wall at Fort MacArthur, and says black soldiers were shipped south.

segments.title: Whether the army scarred Lester
segments.summary: Lee rejects the view that the army permanently broke Lester, saying the effect lasted a year or two.

segments.title: Leonard Feather's claim Lee upbraided Lester
segments.summary: Lee rejects the word upbraiding for his advice to his older brother, saying Lester was an artist and not a businessman.

segments.title: Lee plans to publish Lester's songs to get royalties to his family
segments.summary: Lee says companies exploit deceased musicians without accounting to the estate, and says he will copyright Lester's songs in his Flipside publishing company for Lester Jr.

segments.title: Leaving Nat in 1962 and founding Melic Records
segments.summary: Lee quit playing in 1962 after a stint with Andy Williams and started his record company Melic in July or August.

segments.title: Melic label, Ethel Waters search, and the Damita Jo album
segments.summary: Lee started Melic with publishing companies Flipside and Land Lee, considered recording Ethel Waters, and made an album with Damita Jo.

segments.title: Pressing-plant costs, the Cleveland shipment and independents
segments.summary: Lee describes paying 13 cents a record, shipping 10,000 to Cleveland, and getting back mostly old records instead of sales.

segments.title: Working for Vee-Jay and the Sunset budget line at United Artists
segments.summary: Randy Wood hired Lee at Vee-Jay, which had the first Beatle records; after it closed he ran UA's $1.99 Sunset reissue line.

segments.title: The overnight Oh Happy Day album and moves to Dunhill, ABC and Motown
segments.summary: Lee produced a ten-song gospel album with Oh Happy Day in a weekend for Dunhill, then moved to ABC in 1969 and Motown in 1973 and again in 1977.

segments.title: Son Lee Jr. becomes an entertainment attorney
segments.summary: Lee steered his son toward entertainment law and got him jobs at Universal and then ABC as chief counsel and later Motown.

segments.title: Running recording budgets at Motown
segments.summary: At Motown Lee oversees recording budgets, using his studio experience to argue with artists about numbers of strings, and recalls his ABC soundtrack albums.

segments.title: The planned Motown jazz label and his gospel recording at ABC
segments.summary: Lee says he came to Motown to start a jazz label, and recalls recording gospel for Duke Peacock at ABC.

segments.title: The office view of Capitol and his golf murals
segments.summary: Willard observes the view onto the old Capitol Records building and Lee's golf murals; he declines to discuss the jazz label further.

segments.title: Producing a singer cheaply in Mexico City
segments.summary: Lee recorded a singer in Mexico City for half the Los Angeles cost, with Ernie Freeman's charts, charging only hotel and golf.

segments.title: Cover versions of Billboard's top twelve for Germany and Japan
segments.summary: Lee produced weekly top-twelve cover records for export, such as Honey, and the German studios sent back superior-sounding copies.
